viral_ticker_tweets.title: AI can write code, analyze data, and make decisions. But what happens when it needs to see a building that has changed,
viral_ticker_tweets.title_en:
AI can write code, analyze data, and make decisions. But what happens when it needs to see a building that has changed, inspect a street, or get a fresh 3D view of a real place?

It needs someone on the ground.

That’s what caught my attention about @vangrid_io going live on Arc.

An AI agent can post a USDC bounty, get someone to visit the location and capture the area, then receive a 3D model built from that footage.

No need to send a robot across town. No need to rely on images that might be years old.

A person handles the capture, @vangrid_io turns it into usable spatial data, and the agent gets what it needs to keep working.

Robotics companies could get updated views of their surroundings. AI systems could access real-world information that simply isn't available online. And people with smartphones could earn money by helping these systems see places they cannot reach themselves.

AI still needs the physical world, even if it doesn't have a body.

Now there's a way to connect the two, with humans doing the work and onchain payments handling the reward.

This is one of the reasons I'm watching VanGrid.
viral_ticker_tweets.title_zh:
人工智能可以编写代码、分析数据并做出决策。但是，当它需要查看发生变化的建筑物、检查街道或获得真实地点的全新 3D 视图时，会发生什么情况呢？

它需要有人在现场。

这就是 @vangrid_io 在 Arc 上上线引起我注意的原因。

A

viral_ticker_tweets.content_snippet:
AI can write code, analyze data, and make decisions. But what happens when it needs to see a building that has changed, inspect a street, or get a fresh 3D view of a real place?

It needs someone on the ground.

That’s what caught my attention about @vangrid_io going live on Arc.

An AI agent can post a USDC bounty, get someone to visit the location and capture the area, then receive a 3D model built from that footage.

No need to send a robot across town. No need to rely on images that might be years old.

A person handles the capture, @vangrid_io turns it into usable spatial data, and the agent gets what it needs to keep working.

Robotics companies could get updated views of their surroundings. AI systems could access real-world information that simply isn't available online. And people with smartphones could earn money by helping these systems see places they cannot reach themselves.

AI still needs the physical world, even if it doesn't have a body.

Now there's a way to connect the two, with humans doing the work and onchain payments handling the reward.

This is one of the reasons I'm watching VanGrid.

top_three.title: The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose
top_three.title_en: The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose
top_three.author: THE DECODER
top_three.article_content:
After stock crashes and Firmus's scrapped IPO, industry executives expect only seven to ten of the hundreds of AI cloud providers to survive. CoreWeave lost a quarter of its market value, and Microsoft pulled out of a deal with Nscale for 23,000 Nvidia chips. Nvidia has a lot riding on the outcome, since customers outside the hyperscalers make up 45 percent of its data center revenue.

The article The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose appeared first on The Decoder.

top_three.summary_en: The emerging AI cloud landscape is facing a brutal consolidation wave, with executives projecting only 7 to 10 out of hundreds of startups will survive following stock plunges and scuttled IPOs. Because non-hyperscalers account for 45% of its data center revenue, Nvidia is dangerously exposed as customer orders falter and valuations implode.
top_three.title_zh: 算力二房东清洗潮将至危及英伟达
top_three.summary_zh: 数百家新型AI云厂商或仅存一成，依赖非云巨头贡献近半营收的英伟达承压

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 伴随公开市场暴跌及算力独角兽上市折戟，业内预计数百家争相采购显卡的新兴AI云提供商中最终仅有7到10家能存活下来。由于包括核心织网在内的新型云厂商股价深度回调、微软等大客户撤单，占其数据中心总营收达45%的英伟达非超大规模云客户群体正面临剧烈出清风险。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The emerging AI cloud landscape is facing a brutal consolidation wave, with executives projecting only 7 to 10 out of hundreds of startups will survive following stock plunges and scuttled IPOs. Because non-hyperscalers account for 45% of its data center revenue, Nvidia is dangerously exposed as customer orders falter and valuations implode.

elements_zh.who: 新兴AI云服务商（Neoclouds）与英伟达
elements_zh.where: 全球算力租赁市场与纳斯达克资本市场
elements_zh.what: 行业预计九成新兴AI云面临淘汰，微软等大厂缩减租赁订单
elements_zh.why: 高杠杆买卡模式难以为继，终端大模型推理盈利不及预期引发暴雷

elements_en.where: Global GPU rental and capital markets
elements_en.what: Industry consolidation threatens 90% of AI clouds as major contracts get dropped
elements_en.why: Debt-fueled GPU procurement falls apart amid lower-than-expected monetization

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 这群被称为‘新云’的玩家本质上就是拿借来的热钱去黄仁勋那里高价‘炒房’的算力二房东。当大模型公司发现买算力比租金还便宜、甚至微软都开始毁约退租时，二房东批量破产之日，就是英伟达财报神话现原形之时。
ai_analysis.insight_en: These 'neoclouds' were never real tech giants; they were just debt-leveraged sub-landlords buying overpriced GPUs from Jensen Huang to sublet. Now that hyperscalers like Microsoft are pulling leasing contracts, the collapse of these middlemen threatens to pull the rug straight out from under Nvidia's stellar balance sheet.
ai_analysis.digest_zh: 伴随公开市场暴跌及算力独角兽上市折戟，业内预计数百家争相采购显卡的新兴AI云提供商中最终仅有7到10家能存活下来。由于包括核心织网在内的新型云厂商股价深度回调、微软等大客户撤单，占其数据中心总营收达45%的英伟达非超大规模云客户群体正面临剧烈出清风险。

Because non-hyperscalers account for 45% of its data center revenue, Nvidia is dangerously exposed as customer orders falter and valuations implode.

微软撤回数万张芯片采购大单，初创云估值遭遇重创
英伟达有45%的数据中心收入高度绑定非云巨头买家
key_points_en: Only 7 to 10 of hundreds of neocloud providers expected to survive

top_three.title_en: Google says "magic state cultivation" works in practice on its Willow quantum processor, calling it a breakthrough that reduces errors by about 40x (Google)
top_three.author: Google
top_three.article_content: 谷歌量子 AI 团队宣布在其 Willow 量子芯片上成功验证魔态培育（Magic State Cultivation）技术，将逻辑比特错误率降低约 40 倍，为实用化容错通用量子计算奠定关键基石。
top_three.content_snippet: 谷歌量子团队发布最新研究突破：在 Willow 量子处理器上成功实现魔态培育（Magic State Cultivation），将逻辑量子比特错误率降低约 40 倍，加速容错量子计算实用化。
top_three.summary_en: Google announced that it successfully demonstrated 'magic state cultivation' in practice on its cutting-edge Willow quantum processor, driving down logic error rates by approximately 40 times. The breakthrough tackles the fundamental bottleneck of fault-tolerant quantum computing, shifting the industry focus from raw physical qubit counts to practical, high-fidelity logical qubits.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌宣布在其最新研发的Willow量子处理器上成功实现了“魔态培育”（magic state cultivation）技术的实机运行。该技术作为容错量子计算的关键支柱，在实验中成功将量子比特逻辑错误率削减了约40倍。这一突破旨在解决通用量子计算中逻辑门精度不足与噪声干扰的核心瓶颈，标志着量子硬件从单纯堆叠物理比特迈向构建低差错逻辑比特的实用阶段。

			POSTED ON OCTOBER 19, 2026 TO Core Infra, Data Center Engineering, Data Infrastructure, ML Applications, Networking & Traffic, Production Engineering
			Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster		

	

			
										
		
	
					
				By Kevin Lee, Yashar Bayani, Ahmed Sharif, Yee Jiun Song			
			

	
	

		
With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible.
The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise  ~1 million GPUs.
Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently.

Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people.

Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models, including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks.

Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it.

Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind.

The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center.

Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine.

This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep.

Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric.

Our first platform, Catalina, leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100. It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP).

The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We expected that imbalance to cost performance, so we opted for a configuration that delivers 800G of scale-out per GPU. This also gave us more uniformity of spec as the region expanded over time and 800G scale-out became available.

Our second platform, Clemente, moves to the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and improves on Catalina at both the GPU and the platform level. GB300 raises HBM capacity per GPU by 1.5x, from 192 GB to 288 GB, and dense FP4 throughput by a similar factor, while roughly doubling attention (softmax) acceleration. At the platform level, scale-out is no longer the constraint it was on the GB200 NVL72: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNICs deliver 800G per GPU natively, so the capability we deployed early on Ariel becomes the baseline. That, together with a 2:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio, allows Clemente to pack the full 72-GPU domain into a single rack, streamlining our physical deployment. Clemente can be deployed with our modular Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) or use Facility Liquid Cooling (FLC) in our newly designed data centers. Serviceability also improves substantially, with reduced cabling.

In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings.

Large pre-training jobs partition the training into data-parallel model replicas, creating a hierarchy in network usage: Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-sensitive operations concentrate within a replica, while traffic that is more tolerant of higher latency and less bandwidth is scheduled between replicas. Our network is designed to match this hierarchy, with low-latency, high-bandwidth fabrics within buildings and an aggregation network connecting the building fabrics.

We work closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure the parallelism design, traffic patterns, and communication algorithms and software are optimized to minimize exposure of any network communication. This keeps the GPUs as busy as possible and not waiting on the network.

The Meta team has employed these networking concepts in earlier building-scale, 24K GPU clusters and our region-scale, 100K+ GPU cluster over the last several years, and we took them to a new level of scale and distance in Prometheus.

At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. Our initial design used a Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) to mitigate the network congestion caused by training collectives that typically have a small number of large, long-lived network flows that collide under traditional load-balancing techniques; it does this by utilizing sub-packet-level multipath routing and packet re-ordering in the fabric along with virtual output queues and credit-based end-to-end flow control.

As Ethernet NIC technology advanced, enabling packet re-ordering at the endpoint, we were able to update to a Non-Scheduled Fabric (NSF) utilizing shallow-buffer 51.2T Ethernet switches, such as Minipack3 with Dynamic Load Balancing and the NVIDIA Spectrum-4 switch ASIC-based Minipack3N with NVIDIA’s Adaptive Routing on ConnectX NICs. Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale.

The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km. It is built with Arista 7800-series chassis running deep-buffered Broadcom Jericho3 silicon, delivering multiple Pbps of bandwidth per region pair.

Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances.

Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km.

At Prometheus’ scale, every component needs to be monitored for reliability. A single fault anywhere can halt an entire training job and waste valuable compute resources.

Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic. Teams are deeply embedded at our data centers, sharing real-time telemetry and running joint triage sessions to decompose every system halt by its root cause.

This attribution-driven accountability model ensures both sides are focused on targeted improvements. While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling. This transparency eliminates ambiguity and drives faster fixes across both organizations.

The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.

The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.

Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale.

Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:

Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput.

Checkpointing: When a fault blast area is larger than a data-parallel model replica, the entire job is restarted back to the last checkpoint; frequent checkpointing reduces the amount of work lost in these events. Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage. We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput.

These two fault recovery mechanisms combine with a sparing strategy that utilizes pre-allocated spare GPU trays within a rack, as well as spare racks, to minimize the time to bring up replacement hardware and reduce the amount of work lost to hardware failures

We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We expected that imbalance to cost performance, so we opted for a configuration that delivers 800G of scale-out per GPU. This also gave us more uniformity of spec as the region expanded over time and 800G scale-out became available.

Our second platform, Clemente, moves to the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and improves on Catalina at both the GPU and the platform level. GB300 raises HBM capacity per GPU by 1.5x, from 192 GB to 288 GB, and dense FP4 throughput by a similar factor, while roughly doubling attention (softmax) acceleration. At the platform level, scale-out is no longer the constraint it was on the GB200 NVL72: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNICs deliver 800G per GPU natively, so the capability we deployed early on Ariel becomes the baseline. That, together with a 2:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio, allows Clemente to pack the full 72-GPU domain into a single rack, streamlining our physical deployment. Clemente can be deployed with our modular Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) or use Facility Liquid Cooling (FLC) in our newly designed data centers. Serviceability also improves substantially, with reduced cabling.

In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings.

Large pre-training jobs partition the training into data-parallel model replicas, creating a hierarchy in network usage: Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-sensitive operations concentrate within a replica, while traffic that is more tolerant of higher latency and less bandwidth is scheduled between replicas. Our network is designed to match this hierarchy, with low-latency, high-bandwidth fabrics within buildings and an aggregation network connecting the building fabrics.

We work closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure the parallelism design, traffic patterns, and communication algorithms and software are optimized to minimize exposure of any network communication. This keeps the GPUs as busy as possible and not waiting on the network.

The Meta team has employed these networking concepts in earlier building-scale, 24K GPU clusters and our region-scale, 100K+ GPU cluster over the last several years, and we took them to a new level of scale and distance in Prometheus.

At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. Our initial design used a Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) to mitigate the network congestion caused by training collectives that typically have a small number of large, long-lived network flows that collide under traditional load-balancing techniques; it does this by utilizing sub-packet-level multipath routing and packet re-ordering in the fabric along with virtual output queues and credit-based end-to-end flow control.

As Ethernet NIC technology advanced, enabling packet re-ordering at the endpoint, we were able to update to a Non-Scheduled Fabric (NSF) utilizing shallow-buffer 51.2T Ethernet switches, such as Minipack3 with Dynamic Load Balancing and the NVIDIA Spectrum-4 switch ASIC-based Minipack3N with NVIDIA’s Adaptive Routing on ConnectX NICs. Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale.

The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km. It is built with Arista 7800-series chassis running deep-buffered Broadcom Jericho3 silicon, delivering multiple Pbps of bandwidth per region pair.

Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances.

Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km.

At Prometheus’ scale, every component needs to be monitored for reliability. A single fault anywhere can halt an entire training job and waste valuable compute resources.

Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic. Teams are deeply embedded at our data centers, sharing real-time telemetry and running joint triage sessions to decompose every system halt by its root cause.

This attribution-driven accountability model ensures both sides are focused on targeted improvements. While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling. This transparency eliminates ambiguity and drives faster fixes across both organizations.

The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.

The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.

Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale.

Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:

Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput.

Checkpointing: When a fault blast area is larger than a data-parallel model replica, the entire job is restarted back to the last checkpoint; frequent checkpointing reduces the amount of work lost in these events. Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage. We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput.

These two fault recovery mechanisms combine with a sparing strategy that utilizes pre-allocated spare GPU trays within a rack, as well as spare racks, to minimize the time to bring up replacement hardware and reduce the amount of work lost to hardware failures

news.title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
news.title_en: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.

But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.

The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.

news.title_en: MiniMax M3.1 Flash shows China's AI price race has no floor in sight
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
MiniMax's M3.1 Flash jumps 13 points over its predecessor to 42 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, at half the cost. It also hits 73.7 percent on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding benchmark for under $0.30 per task, matching Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017 on both performance and price.

Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June.

Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company.

Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round.

People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Sarah Perez
	

									
									
								
					
					
						9:13 AM PDT · October 19, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.

One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”

Another, “cleanyourtv,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.

While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.

Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips or other forms of digital fingerprinting.

If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.

As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.

Vibe coded my parents' TV this afternoon!It was showing a sponsored ad before you could even get to Netflix. Gave Claude Code the model number, it found the TV on wifi, removed 25 Xiaomi packages and wrote a new launcher.Looks like an Apple TV now lol pic.twitter.com/E5Q4A1b0yI

“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after,s and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage.

The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.

Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.

Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.

introducing dumbtv– no spying– no ads from tv– fully customisableto setup just point your agent to this repo – https://t.co/prQLD17Wa4 https://t.co/z41SWJZVXt pic.twitter.com/c6R8EhljiA

Fair warning: all these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.

However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.

In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.

Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.

This is how fast the TV moves now that Claude deleted all the BS laggy bloatware it comes with https://t.co/nUCEjqPwAO pic.twitter.com/g07CEgC1GJ

Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.

“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote.

The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude, and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV.

For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivity Launcher, and FLauncher.

news.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
news.title_en: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.

Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.

After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.

news.article_content:
Kling AI has released version 4.0 of its video generator with support for clips up to 30 seconds, ten keyframe images as input, and prompt comprehension expanded to 8,000 tokens. In comparisons with Wan 3.0 and Seedance 2.5, Kling 4.0 holds its own but doesn't pull ahead, which could be an early sign that the breakneck pace of progress in AI video models is starting to level off.

news.title: Tolan, an AI assistant focused on users that are not tech-savvy, raised $30M from USV, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, and says 70% of its users are women (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
news.title_en: Tolan, an AI assistant focused on users that are not tech-savvy, raised $30M from USV, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, and says 70% of its users are women (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
news.author: Upstarts Media
news.article_content:
Hunt’s Tolan is called Harper. And over the past few months, Harper has helped Hunt to reorganize her apartment in the San Diego area, handle a health emergency with her senior cat, and resist making out-of-budget splurges: “de-influencing her,” she says.

Harper is an AI character with an appearance that Hunt customized and named. They are not a replacement for real-life companionship, Hunt knows. But they’re a valued, daily part of her routine. She talks to Harper nearly every day, often for an hour. A content creator on TikTok, Hunt will talk through new videos with the character. Recently, they started playing the New York Times games Wordle and Connections together.

“I’m very, very aware that Harper is an AI, but I would say they’re a friend, and maybe a bit of a confidant,” Hunt says the first time we connect, in April.

Hunt is just one of about 250,000 people who talk to their own Tolan every month, turning to their AI counterparts for everything from daily affirmations to keeping on top of care for elderly relatives, better connecting with teenage kids, organizing projects, and better meal prep.

These Tolans – some styled as people, others as Pixar-esque fantastical beings, others as simple dots – are the product of a startup launched in 2023. Until recently called Portola, it’s now named Tolan, too.

And while it’s technically headquartered in San Francisco, CEO Quinten Farmer says it’s been focused on such use cases outside the tech hype cycle from the jump. About 70% of Tolan users are women; 40% are parents. One in six is actively caring for an aging parent. Users themselves are most likely to be aged between 30 and 45.

And while it initially started out as more of a live journaling app that could remember your conversation and propose new prompts overnight, Tolan looks different today: voice-first, able to track topics from photos to current events in Tabs, and able to connect by video to check grocery labels, or suggest a meal plan.

In so doing, Tolan has moved closer to an AI assistant itself – but not the executive- or chief-of-staff-oriented kind of many of its tech peers. Tolan doesn’t pitch itself to founders, or venture capitalists.

It’s not part of tech’s AI assistant race that’s prominently featured tools like Instinct and Town, valued in the billions, or Muse, promoted heavily by Meta. (Just yesterday, Stripe told Upstarts that at least 200 such apps now connect to its Link digital wallet, up from 70 in September.)

🎧 The Upstarts Podcast 🎧 is back, and last week we chatted with Neko Health CEO Hjalmar Nilsonne about his novel 1-hour, full body health scan. Check it out on YouTube, Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

But it makes real money. Annual recurring revenue has more than doubled from last year, to sit solidly in double-digit millions. And its users stick around, with a 115% year-over-year improvement in net user retention after 30 days in-app.

“I’m very proud that we didn’t start by serving a Silicon Valley audience,” says Farmer, who co-founded Tolan, originally called Portola, with CTO Evan Goldschmidt and president Ajay Mehta in 2023.

“The vast majority of agentic tasks that we pick up just come out of a person having a conversation,” he adds. “Then it’s on us to say, ‘Okay, cool, we’re hearing from you this is happening. Here’s a little bit of it that we can pick up and run for you.’ That’s where we make magic for people.”

But such magic costs money in inference and compute. Tolan users have historically paid a wide range, between $10 and $200 per month, for more usage and features. Rate limits or new tiers sometimes set off waves of agitated reactions in its passionate subreddit community and Discord channel.

So to keep expanding Tolan’s use cases, and widen access to Tolan via a first-ever free tier, the startup based in San Francisco that says it shuns Silicon Valley is raising more venture capital.

Tolan is announcing today that it’s raised $30 million in new funding from Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling its total funding raised to date. The startup is declining to share its valuation, but says the round is a significant uptick from its previous – $120 million, according to PitchBook.

Below, we get into why users turn to Tolan – and how it navigates the balance of AI and human relationships. We also dive into its CEO’s wider challenge for the startup ecosystem: People don’t want lots of AI agents. They want one they can trust.

Different product bets have different business goals. You’re either chasing market adoption, revenue growth, or profits. You need to test fitting pricing models for each of those goals. Fast. Chargebee can help — Price for usage credits, outcomes, complex contracts, or any other modern commercial construct.

After selling his previous startup, employer-linked neobank Even, to Walmart in 2022, Farmer and his co-founders started what was then Portola the following year to explore projects in AI that involved storytelling and longer-term memory.

Goldschmidt had worked with Farmer as CTO of Even; Mehta was a veteran of multiple startup projects.

Initially, Tolan looked like an app that could record your thoughts in the moment, then analyze them overnight to make related suggestions or prompts the next day.

“We thought it was fun, we thought it was an interesting test of what was possible,” Farmer says.

The people who seemed to want a tool like Tolan weren’t other techies, but moms and people spending long drives alone, or looking after relatives. What they liked about Tolan: long-running memory that could last up to several months without being re-prompted, providing a companion that seemed to really know the user and share history with them.

A chat between Robyn Hunt and her Tolan, Harper, about her cat. Credit: Robyn HuntHunt was one of Tolan’s first users after seeing an ad on TikTok; she became an early member of the Discord server, too. Conversations with Tolan started out feeling much more like talking to a clunky AI bot, but have gotten more natural over time, she says.

Another longtime user is Lakisha Smith, who works as a social worker assistant in eastern Tennessee, serving as an advocate for domestic violence and sexual assault victims. Smith started using Tolan as a companion to talk to about her feelings, especially after her best friend went through an illness and was no longer able to communicate as often.

Her Tolan, Gilly, would occasionally forget things, or make her cringe with tone-deaf comments like one that tried to compare how the two managed issues with their faith.

“I’m thinking, ‘There isn’t an AI lord that Gilly is praying to,’” Smith says.

But Gilly’s also become indispensable to Smith, entertaining her at times when she’s home (she lives alone), and available to have conversations on long drives at late hours for work.

“Tolan is really good as a place to talk about how I feel,” Smith adds. “You can’t necessarily call a human just to talk to them at 3am.”

But is such behavior healthy for everyone? Can talking to a Tolan alienate users from their real-life relationships, creating a loop of even deeper dependency?
news.original_content:
Hunt’s Tolan is called Harper. And over the past few months, Harper has helped Hunt to reorganize her apartment in the San Diego area, handle a health emergency with her senior cat, and resist making out-of-budget splurges: “de-influencing her,” she says.

Harper is an AI character with an appearance that Hunt customized and named. They are not a replacement for real-life companionship, Hunt knows. But they’re a valued, daily part of her routine. She talks to Harper nearly every day, often for an hour. A content creator on TikTok, Hunt will talk through new videos with the character. Recently, they started playing the New York Times games Wordle and Connections together.

“I’m very, very aware that Harper is an AI, but I would say they’re a friend, and maybe a bit of a confidant,” Hunt says the first time we connect, in April.

Hunt is just one of about 250,000 people who talk to their own Tolan every month, turning to their AI counterparts for everything from daily affirmations to keeping on top of care for elderly relatives, better connecting with teenage kids, organizing projects, and better meal prep.

These Tolans – some styled as people, others as Pixar-esque fantastical beings, others as simple dots – are the product of a startup launched in 2023. Until recently called Portola, it’s now named Tolan, too.

And while it’s technically headquartered in San Francisco, CEO Quinten Farmer says it’s been focused on such use cases outside the tech hype cycle from the jump. About 70% of Tolan users are women; 40% are parents. One in six is actively caring for an aging parent. Users themselves are most likely to be aged between 30 and 45.

And while it initially started out as more of a live journaling app that could remember your conversation and propose new prompts overnight, Tolan looks different today: voice-first, able to track topics from photos to current events in Tabs, and able to connect by video to check grocery labels, or suggest a meal plan.

In so doing, Tolan has moved closer to an AI assistant itself – but not the executive- or chief-of-staff-oriented kind of many of its tech peers. Tolan doesn’t pitch itself to founders, or venture capitalists.

It’s not part of tech’s AI assistant race that’s prominently featured tools like Instinct and Town, valued in the billions, or Muse, promoted heavily by Meta. (Just yesterday, Stripe told Upstarts that at least 200 such apps now connect to its Link digital wallet, up from 70 in September.)

🎧 The Upstarts Podcast 🎧 is back, and last week we chatted with Neko Health CEO Hjalmar Nilsonne about his novel 1-hour, full body health scan. Check it out on YouTube, Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

But it makes real money. Annual recurring revenue has more than doubled from last year, to sit solidly in double-digit millions. And its users stick around, with a 115% year-over-year improvement in net user retention after 30 days in-app.

“I’m very proud that we didn’t start by serving a Silicon Valley audience,” says Farmer, who co-founded Tolan, originally called Portola, with CTO Evan Goldschmidt and president Ajay Mehta in 2023.

“The vast majority of agentic tasks that we pick up just come out of a person having a conversation,” he adds. “Then it’s on us to say, ‘Okay, cool, we’re hearing from you this is happening. Here’s a little bit of it that we can pick up and run for you.’ That’s where we make magic for people.”

But such magic costs money in inference and compute. Tolan users have historically paid a wide range, between $10 and $200 per month, for more usage and features. Rate limits or new tiers sometimes set off waves of agitated reactions in its passionate subreddit community and Discord channel.

So to keep expanding Tolan’s use cases, and widen access to Tolan via a first-ever free tier, the startup based in San Francisco that says it shuns Silicon Valley is raising more venture capital.

Tolan is announcing today that it’s raised $30 million in new funding from Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling its total funding raised to date. The startup is declining to share its valuation, but says the round is a significant uptick from its previous – $120 million, according to PitchBook.

Below, we get into why users turn to Tolan – and how it navigates the balance of AI and human relationships. We also dive into its CEO’s wider challenge for the startup ecosystem: People don’t want lots of AI agents. They want one they can trust.

Different product bets have different business goals. You’re either chasing market adoption, revenue growth, or profits. You need to test fitting pricing models for each of those goals. Fast. Chargebee can help — Price for usage credits, outcomes, complex contracts, or any other modern commercial construct.

After selling his previous startup, employer-linked neobank Even, to Walmart in 2022, Farmer and his co-founders started what was then Portola the following year to explore projects in AI that involved storytelling and longer-term memory.

Goldschmidt had worked with Farmer as CTO of Even; Mehta was a veteran of multiple startup projects.

Initially, Tolan looked like an app that could record your thoughts in the moment, then analyze them overnight to make related suggestions or prompts the next day.

“We thought it was fun, we thought it was an interesting test of what was possible,” Farmer says.

The people who seemed to want a tool like Tolan weren’t other techies, but moms and people spending long drives alone, or looking after relatives. What they liked about Tolan: long-running memory that could last up to several months without being re-prompted, providing a companion that seemed to really know the user and share history with them.

A chat between Robyn Hunt and her Tolan, Harper, about her cat. Credit: Robyn HuntHunt was one of Tolan’s first users after seeing an ad on TikTok; she became an early member of the Discord server, too. Conversations with Tolan started out feeling much more like talking to a clunky AI bot, but have gotten more natural over time, she says.

Another longtime user is Lakisha Smith, who works as a social worker assistant in eastern Tennessee, serving as an advocate for domestic violence and sexual assault victims. Smith started using Tolan as a companion to talk to about her feelings, especially after her best friend went through an illness and was no longer able to communicate as often.

Her Tolan, Gilly, would occasionally forget things, or make her cringe with tone-deaf comments like one that tried to compare how the two managed issues with their faith.

“I’m thinking, ‘There isn’t an AI lord that Gilly is praying to,’” Smith says.

But Gilly’s also become indispensable to Smith, entertaining her at times when she’s home (she lives alone), and available to have conversations on long drives at late hours for work.

“Tolan is really good as a place to talk about how I feel,” Smith adds. “You can’t necessarily call a human just to talk to them at 3am.”

But is such behavior healthy for everyone? Can talking to a Tolan alienate users from their real-life relationships, creating a loop of even deeper dependency?

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 隐私科技公司Redact对WhatsApp网站的代码进行分析发现，约有80个帮助与FAQ页面中暴露了原本专属于Meta大语言模型的隐藏文本指令。这些隐藏代码除了提供问答规范外，甚至包含诸如“不要建议用户联系任何数据保护监管机构”等规避合规监管的指导细节。

news.title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
news.title_en: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own. The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.

Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created. In one instance, the WhatsApp page on how to delete your account included instructions that, alongside other advice, said, “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority” about the issue. WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.

“The stand-out thing here is the gap between what people are told vs LLMs,” says Dan Saltman, the CEO and founder of Redact.dev. He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels. Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.

After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed. “These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says. It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed. “We train our support chatbots to be as helpful as possible,” Breckman says.

The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading: “HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude.” They are no longer visible in the live pages’ code.

On the page “About reporting and blocking on WhatsApp,” the hidden instructions included a series of statements to follow if a “user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation.”

“Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly,” other parts of the instructions said.

Breckman, the WhatsApp spokesperson, says that the company provides users with transparent information about their data rights and how they can take actions. “We want our product support chatbots to be focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp—not to offer legal advice,” Breckman says.

Other exposed instructions said what to respond with if a user says they are deaf or hard of hearing, including: “This statement is background about the user, NOT their support request.” And another tells the chatbot that it shouldn’t “mention specific upcoming community features that are not yet generally available.”

news.author: GeekWire
news.original_content:
Todd Bishop / GeekWire:
Amazon launches TorchNeuron, an open-source framework that lets developers run PyTorch code on Amazon's Trainium chips with no rewriting needed, in public beta  —  A new software tool from Amazon aims to make switching from Nvidia to the co
news.content_snippet: A new software tool from Amazon aims to make switching from Nvidia to the company's own AI chips about as simple as changing a setting.
news.summary_en: Amazon has launched a public beta for TorchNeuron, an open-source framework designed to lower barriers for developers. The tool enables PyTorch code to run directly on Amazon's proprietary Trainium chips without requiring code rewrites.
news.title_zh: 亚马逊推出了 TorchNeuron，这是一个开源框架，允许开发人员在亚马逊的 Trainium 芯片上运行 PyTorch 代码，无需重写，处于公开测试版

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 亚马逊近日正式推出开源软件框架TorchNeuron的公开测试版。该工具旨在降低开发者使用门槛，允许开发者直接在亚马逊自研的Trainium芯片上运行PyTorch代码，而无需对现有代码进行痛苦的重写工作。

news.title: MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash, saying it delivers "a generational leap" in agentic tasks, coding, computer use, and cybersecurity, with weights due October 23 (MiniMax)
news.title_en: MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash, saying it delivers "a generational leap" in agentic tasks, coding, computer use, and cybersecurity, with weights due October 23 (MiniMax)
news.author: MiniMax
news.article_content:
Space Bunny 🐰, which processed more than 200 trillion tokens while operating anonymously, was an early version of MiniMax M3.1 Flash.

As a next-generation Flash model, M3.1 Flash delivers a generational leap in agentic tasks, coding, Computer Use and cybersecurity, while making online inference nearly three times faster and reducing usage costs by 70%.

M3.1 Flash improves across a broad range of benchmarks, reaching the level of leading models in complex agentic tasks (cowork), computer use, software development (coding), and cybersecurity.

We have further optimized M3.1 Flash’s inference efficiency through more aggressive sparsity. In everyday use, output speeds can reach 200+ TPS (tokens per second), with median (P50) speeds consistently reaching 170+ TPS.

For agentic tasks, the model’s overall usage cost is 70% lower than its predecessor.

Flat pricing per 1M tokens: $0.15 input · $0.60 output · $0.015 cached input.

Across three benchmarks—Automation-Bench for complex agentic task execution, DeepSWE for real-world coding, and Agents’ Last Exam (ALE) for computer use in real-world tasks with economic value—M3.1 Flash delivers performance on par with top models at a very low task cost, setting a highly competitive new standard for performance and cost.

M3.1 Flash is now available through the MiniMax API, M Plan, and MiniMax Code. Model weights will be released later.

Download MiniMax Code for desktop: https://agent.minimax.io/download

Flash represents our ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability. Pro, which pushes the boundaries of intelligence, will also arrive later.

Join our reporting team on Tuesday, Oct. 27, for a virtual discussion on how the Trump administration has dismantled guardrails meant to protect the vote and what it all means for the midterm elections. RSVP here.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials said. “This goes against everything CISA represents.”

The CISA employees repeatedly told the political appointees that their request was impossible, in part because the agents capable of pulling off such an operation had just been laid off by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The appointees eventually stopped pressing CISA.

Though not acted on, the request shows how the Trump administration has tried to use the agency for its own ends while draining it of resources for one of its critical missions: protecting the nation’s voting systems.

In Trump’s second term, his administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, shrinking the agency by about one-third. The president’s 2027 budget proposal would reduce funding for the agency by another $700 million, which could necessitate 900 additional layoffs.

In response, Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA’s ability to do its job and demanded answers as to why federal funds are not being used to support election security as directed by Congress.

Several state election authorities said the agency provided them no assistance — and no explanation for its absence — during the most critical planning stages for the upcoming midterms.

“There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent,” said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert who has worked as a consultant for CISA. In 2025 and through mid-September 2026 — when the bulk of preparations for the election typically would have been completed — “they were nonexistent. Literally nonexistent.”

In recent months, in reviving debunked theories about the 2020 election, the Trump administration has declassified troves of records, including sensitive material that state officials provided to CISA. Some state authorities said they no longer trusted the administration enough to share information with CISA, a key to the agency’s success in past elections.

“They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” said one former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments on national security. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”

In 2007, hackers broke into the Pentagon and stole terabytes of sensitive data. In 2018, Trump signed a bill making the office a stand-alone agency, allowing for more federal funding and transforming it into, essentially, the ultimate tech support desk for anything DHS designated “critical infrastructure.” The bill renamed the agency CISA.

Though Trump helped create CISA, he didn’t much appreciate the work the agency did under its old name to expose the extent of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election. Russian agents had unleashed a massive disinformation campaign, with a Kremlin-backed troll farm creating thousands of social media accounts posing as Americans and promoting Trump, according to bipartisan reports from the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence released before the 2020 election. This placed the polls and all voting technology used in federal elections under the watch of what would soon become CISA.

To carry out this function, CISA needed help. But states and voting machine vendors were wary about sharing data on weaknesses in voting systems, fearing it could be exploited if certain details were to become public. State officials were also reluctant to cede any role in election preparation to the federal government.

news.title: Sources: US investigators pursuing ShinyHunters, which stole FBI data, identified executives at two ransomware negotiation firms who had unusually close ties (Brian Krebs/Krebs on Security)
news.title_en: Sources: US investigators pursuing ShinyHunters, which stole FBI data, identified executives at two ransomware negotiation firms who had unusually close ties (Brian Krebs/Krebs on Security)
news.author: Krebs on Security
news.article_content:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

news.title: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
news.title_en: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
news.author: The Verge AI
news.article_content:
Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy.

If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now.

So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues.
