news.title: Filing: US prosecutors say OpenAI suspect Abdulrahman Alfozan maintained frequent WhatsApp contact in 2025 and 2026 with an unnamed Saudi Royal Family member (Dan Mangan/CNBC)
news.title_en: Filing: US prosecutors say OpenAI suspect Abdulrahman Alfozan maintained frequent WhatsApp contact in 2025 and 2026 with an unnamed Saudi Royal Family member (Dan Mangan/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
Federal prosecutors in a new court filing warned that the alleged bugging of an OpenAI executive conference room by a Saudi national working as an engineer at that artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."

Prosecutors in the filing said "OpenAI executives met with government officials" in OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters in the same conference room on days close to when it is alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan  on Sept. 28.

The filing came as Alfozan, 35, faces a detention hearing in U.S. District Court in San Francisco on Monday. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California is asking a judge to keep Alfozan held without bail.

"This is an ongoing investigation that may yet result in more serious charges," the filing says.

The filing cites his ties to Saudi Arabia, his financial resources, and the fact that his wife and their 3-month-old baby flew there on the heels of his Oct. 9 arrest.

Alfozan's lawyer, in a court filing, said the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles offered to cover the full bail for him if a judge agrees to release him on bond. A letter from the consulate was included in a motion for pretrial release by the lawyer.

Magistrate Judge Alex Tse at Monday's hearing questioned the idea of the consulate guaranteeing the bail.

"I find that problematic," Tse said. "It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out.'"

"So the Saudi government is saying, 'We'll take care of everything, we'll have supervision, we will pay the bond, we're not going to approve any travel documents.' But what confidence do I have that they're going to protect the interests of the [U.S.] government?" Tse asked. "That he's not going to flee. He doesn't have to go all the way to Saudi Arabia. He just has to go to Canada or Mexico ... I don't see how that is in his favor.

Source: U.S. District Court in San Francisco, U.S. v. Alfozan.Prosecutors in their detention memo said Alfozan had been "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026.

Alfozan communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say how Alfozan knew that person.

"Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing says.

"In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote.

"The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."

The filing does not say the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from the AI giant.

Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined the firm as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.

Prosecutors in the same filing said the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said.

Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. OpenAI fired him after his arrest.

Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, in a separate filing asked that the defendant be released with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."

The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13.

FBI Director Kash Patel, when Alfozan's arrest was announced, said he allegedly concealed the recording device to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's artificial intelligence technology.

Prosecutors in their new filing also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk because of his access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said.

"He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.

For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit participating units, the filing said.

Alfozan planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

"On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing said.

The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.

news.summary_en: Microsoft has unveiled new security tools within its 365 E7 bundle and the Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats through risk assessments. news.title: Stripe says AI agent purchases are adding up, but it won't share the numbers
news.title_en: Stripe says AI agent purchases are adding up, but it won't share the numbers
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
AI agents are increasingly using Stripe's payment service Link to shop for their users, Upstarts Media reports. In September, the number of transactions grew 38-fold and payment volume grew 20-fold. Stripe hasn't disclosed how many purchases or how much money are behind those figures. According to the report, the growth started from a small base, so it says little about the actual scale. Stripe executive Dan Hill says the volume is now becoming significant, though.

About 70 agents were using the service when Stripe ran the analysis. Hill says that number has since grown to around 200, including Meta's Muse and Grok Bot. Most agents spend about $100 per transaction, according to Hill, but some users have them book flights or buy furniture worth thousands of dollars. Retail made up 36 percent of transactions and 32 percent of volume. Travel came next with 28 percent of volume.

Link doesn't give agents the user's real credit card number. Instead, it issues a separate 16-digit number, and users can set spending limits. Anthropic and OpenAI also use Link, but not yet for agent purchases. Hill admits Stripe won't stay the only option and names PayPal and Shopify's Shop Pay as competitors. He says the market is still in its very early days.AdAd

news.title: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
news.title_en: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.

Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases.

news.title: The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose
news.title_en: The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose
news.author: THE DECODER
news.article_content:
After stock crashes and Firmus's scrapped IPO, industry executives expect only seven to ten of the hundreds of AI cloud providers to survive. CoreWeave lost a quarter of its market value, and Microsoft pulled out of a deal with Nscale for 23,000 Nvidia chips. Nvidia has a lot riding on the outcome, since customers outside the hyperscalers make up 45 percent of its data center revenue.

The article The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose appeared first on The Decoder.

news.title: Analysis: companies are set for a massive acceleration of 50GW+ in data center capacity additions in 2027; 24GW+ across 40 campuses are in the advanced stages (Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros/SemiAnalysis)
news.title_en: Analysis: companies are set for a massive acceleration of 50GW+ in data center capacity additions in 2027; 24GW+ across 40 campuses are in the advanced stages (Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros/SemiAnalysis)
news.author: SemiAnalysis
news.article_content:
It’s very tempting to cede to the FUD given all the constraints on the datacenter buildout: power, labor, supply chains, capital, and many more. But at SemiAnalysis, we care about the truth, not about narratives. And here’s the truth for you: one picture, >24GW of datacenters in advanced stage of construction, all to be delivered in 2027. Most of them are more than halfway done, with exterior cooling and electrical equipment already installed. That’s just 40 campuses, a tiny share of the multiple hundred sites in advanced stage of construction. We track them all, and for the full granularity, use our Datacenter Industry Model.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelOf course, there are plenty of challenges and shortages. Behind these pictures, there are labor issues, supply chain delays, fundraising challenges, among many others. We’ve written in-depth about Modular Datacenters and Labor, Datacenter Electrical systems, Cooling systems, Behind-The-Meter power, the US Grid Constraints, and Nvidia’s ecosystem financial support. But the fact is simple: gigantic sites are simply getting built, and many are on time. For example, just go look at what Crusoe built in Abilene, what AWS built in Indiana, or QTS/Microsoft’s giant site in Georgia. These are the sites that have produced SOTA technology like GPT-6 and Fable 5.5. Looking ahead, despite all the constraints, an accelerating number of giant sites keep getting built, as shown by our Top 40 picture

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelIf you ask any datacenter builder, they’ll tell you how hard it is, how some workers aren’t showing up, how vendors are delayed, and many other issues. All of this is accurate. And that’s why we’ve successfully called out countless datacenter delays and keep calling out developer timelines that appear overly aggressive in our Datacenter model, including the Oracle New Mexico Force Majure site delay in April. To be fair, +50GW is essentially the global cumulative datacenter market up through 2024 being built in one year! But our Datacenter Industry Model adjusts for all of that and still points to a material acceleration in datacenter capacity in 2027. So, what are we seeing that others can’t?

Let’s dig in. We’ll explore the following topics in this report:

SemiAnalysis proprietary leading indicators: we’ll show a sneak peak of our proprietary data supporting our forecast, such as self-build construction starts and datacenter leasing (in MWs and USD). Year-to-date, slightly under USD 1T of binding / non-cancellable datacenter leases have been signed – that’s key to supporting our aggressive 2027-28 forecast.

The shape of the buildout: how can we support +50GW in a single year? Where, what design, what power solutions?

The “real” question: are we going to face a datacenter oversupply? As we explained in The Great Silicon Shortage, datacenters & power may be the tip of the iceberg, with memory and logic possibly becoming the new #1 constraint in 2027-28.

Overall, we are very excited about 2027. The natural implication of the acceleration will be significantly more compute supply. That means cheaper and smarter AI, faster pace of AI model progress, and likely material revenue acceleration for leading AI labs and other token vendors. That also means unthinkable capex numbers. Reflexively rates will have to shoot up to enable the buildouts from a capital demand perspective. Let’s dive in!

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelThe second indicator is Datacenter Leasing. We’ve talked about this a lot in prior reports, but as a quick recap: given the capital-intensity of building multi hundred MW datacenters, developers typically only spend 5-10% of project capital without a customer. They need a “pre-lease” to fund and develop the whole project. That’s typically a 15-20 year contract, with a TCV of $30-50B per GW. Check out our HPC Lease Tracker as part of the Datacenter Model to dive into actual contract economics.

Since H2 2025, things have dramatically changed. Oracle kicked off the era of gigantic leases, after closing on ~4.5GW of datacenter IT capacity across three sites between August and October 2025. Everyone else followed, and the pool of buyers has never been broader, with Meta, AWS, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, AMD, Anthropic and OpenAI all being in the market for GW-scale leases. There’s also a long tail of Neoclouds signing hundred-MW-scale deals.

In USD terms, this means an unprecedented amount of lease value that builders can use to raise debt. Just in 2026 year-to-date, we’ve identified over a trillion USD of lease value that was signed and closed. That trillion is supporting a gigantic datacenter buildout in 2027-28. Our new Compute, Capital & Markets Model is now tracking all the debt raises and can confirm that most of this debt has been raised.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelThe shape of the buildout: how to build 50GW in a yearTracking all of these leading indicators has enabled us to forecast, before anyone else, the upcoming surge in orders for many industrial suppliers like Vertiv, ABB, Sterling Infrastructure. Check out our Industrials Model for in-depth coverage. However, the challenge is now going from orders to delivery. And resources have obviously become constrained, as power, labor, and sheer regulatory overhead are enormous burdens for developers. But the industry has promptly reacted with innovation.

The first step is to simplify datacenter designs. We show below how Google has modularized their electrical architecture, removing a significant amount of outdoors cabling that requires onsite assembly, replacing them with prefabricated electrical modules. We track all the equipment changes (including suppliers) for datacenter designs and forecast orders in our Industrials Model

Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials ModelOthers have opted for more radical design changes. One example is Meta with its tent design, that we exclusively unveiled over a year ago. Another one is AWS which has materially simplified their shell design and launched a new rapid design dubbed “SAMDC”. Data halls are also increasingly prefabricated, an effort called Project Houdini at AWS. Construction timelines are now under 10 months. Hence our “LEGO Datacenters” title for the modular movement, you literally slot them in and go, and doing so allows for MEP labor (7-11 months of work) to drop up to 63%! We will have a full deep dive on the labor of the 2027 buildout coming soon.

Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials ModelIn addition to hyperscale selfbuild, datacenter developers promoting prefabricated designs have also been remarkably successful. DayOne is likely the best example. With a total of ~3GW leased since their first deal in early 2023, the Singaporean company has been a rocket ship in terms of construction speed. While traditional developers have >18 months build timelines, DayOne cut this to ~9 months, which was key to signing huge deals with Firmus, OpenAI and Nvidia.

Source: SemiAnalysis Energy ModelIn addition, the buildout is now geographically diversifying. This naturally bypasses US labor, power, and (in some countries) permitting constraints. And as shown below, the ex-US buildout is sharply accelerating in 2027, and we expect it to gain a lot of market share in 2028, largely driven by US challenges.

Anthropic wants to put five percent of its shares into a new public benefit fund that will also look into direct payments to workers at risk of losing their jobs. This study is Pew Research Center’s latest effort to explore how Americans use and view artificial intelligence (AI). The study also dives into who uses chatbots and has smart home devices with AI features. It also explores what impact people think AI will have on society and on them, personally.

The Center conducts research to inform the public, journalists and decision-makers. Tracking the rise of AI in society has been a key priority for us over the years. It’s important to understand how people use AI in their lives and how they feel these tools will impact themselves and society.

We surveyed 5,119 U.S. adults from Feb. 17 to 23, 2026. Everyone who took part in this survey is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP). The survey represents the views of the full U.S. adult population. Here are the questions used for this report, the topline and the survey methodology.

Does gender factor into how people use and think about artificial intelligence (AI)? In some ways, it does.

Men report using chatbots more regularly than women and are more likely to turn to them for a variety of things, including work. Women, on the other hand, are more skeptical about AI, including how it will impact their own lives.

This work is part of a Pew Research Center survey on Americans’ views of and experiences with AI, conducted Feb. 17-23, 2026. Read the main story to learn more.

Along with tracking use of chatbots overall, we also looked at which platforms men and women turn to.

Men stand out for their use of some specific brands. For example, men are more likely than women to say they ever use Copilot (22% vs. 13%).

Larger shares of men than women also report using Gemini, Grok and Claude.

ChatGPT – the most widely used chatbot in our survey – is used by identical shares of men and women.

On a broad level, men and women tend to use chatbots for similar reasons, with search and work tasks (for those who are employed) topping the list for both groups. But there are some modest differences in what they go to chatbots for.

In several categories, men are somewhat more likely than women to say they use chatbots. These include searching for information, work tasks, fun or entertainment or getting news.

Women are slightly more likely than men to say they use chatbots for emotional support or advice. There are no gender differences in reporting using chatbots for companionship.

In addition to understanding how men and women are using chatbots, we also wanted to understand if they felt differently about whether they’ve found these tools helpful or not.

Men are more likely to say chatbots are helpful for their productivity. While 35% of men say these tools help their productivity, the share drops to 25% among women.

There are modest or no gender differences in how people view chatbots’ impact on their knowledge, creativity, happiness or personal relationships.

Chatbots tell one part of the AI adoption story, but there’s also a range of things people incorporate in their lives and homes that use AI.

Across our surveys, there’s a consistent pattern where women tend to view AI more negatively than men. These gender differences also show up in other surveys of teenagers and AI experts.

In our new survey, women are about twice as likely to say AI will have a negative impact on them personally over the next 20 years than a positive one (33% vs. 17%).

Men, by comparison, are more evenly split. Roughly an equal share of men predict positive outcomes as negative ones.

When it comes to its societal impact, 43% of women expect AI will affect society negatively. Far fewer think it will be positive for society.

While men’s views about societal impact also tilt negative, the gap is not as large.

We also asked the public if AI was advancing too quickly, too slowly, or at the right pace and found some gender differences there as well.

Majorities of Americans believe AI is moving too fast, but women are more likely than men to say this (68% vs. 58%).

Relatively few Americans believe AI is moving too slowly, but men are about 10 percentage points more likely than women to think it’s advancing at the right pace.

As AI rapidly evolves, there have been more conversations about and efforts to increase the public’s understanding of the technology.

Just as with certain uses and views, men and women also differ in their familiarity and confidence in using AI.

Nearly all men and women today have some familiarity with AI. But men are more likely to say they’ve heard a lot about the technology.

Just over half of men say they’ve heard a lot about AI overall, compared with 41% of women.

news.summary_en: A new survey of over 5,000 U.S. adults reveals that the overall gender adoption gap for chatbots has closed since 2024, with mainstream tools seeing identical usage rates across genders. However, men remain significantly more likely to use them on a daily basis, highlighting persistent disparities in high-frequency productivity engagement. The shift marks AI's evolution from a niche tech toy to a widespread utility, even as daily habit loops diverge.

ai_analysis.insight_en: On paper, the gender divide has vanished, but behind the scenes, men are still treating chatbots as 24/7 digital crutches and unpaid interns. Everyone knows how to polish an email with AI now, but daily obsession with automated reality remains heavily skewed.

Foxconn agrees to acquire a 50% stake in Mitsubishi's automotive components unit for ~$727M; Mitsubishi will provide autonomous tech for Foxconn's EV platforms  —  Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. is paying ¥115 billion ($727 million)
news.content_snippet: Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. is paying ¥115 billion ($727 million) for a 50% stake in Mitsubishi Electric Corp.'s automotive-components unit …

news.title: Elon Musk says "I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America" in 2027; at SpaceX's $146.03 Friday close, the gift would be valued at ~$10.5B (Kai Nicol-Schwarz/CNBC)
news.title_en: Elon Musk says "I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America" in 2027; at SpaceX's $146.03 Friday close, the gift would be valued at ~$10.5B (Kai Nicol-Schwarz/CNBC)
news.author: CNBC
news.article_content:
SpaceX boss Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.

Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.

There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.

That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.

"This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.

Musk's comments come hot on the heels of Anthropic revealing that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.

In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing.

Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.

news.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
news.title_en: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.

The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.

A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.

news.summary_en: Environmental field researchers in Alaska are conducting rigorous surveys across boreal wildfire scars to assess the deepening threat to the Arctic's subterranean carbon reservoirs. Intensifying heatwaves and prolonged droughts are allowing lightning-sparked blazes to consume the protective moss canopy and penetrate deep permafrost soils. This subterranean combustion risks unlocking millions of tons of prehistoric greenhouse gases, threatening an irreversible feedback loop in global climate modeling.
news.title_zh: 北极野火威胁远古冻土引发全球碳爆发风险
news.summary_zh: 科研团队深入阿拉斯加森林前线，追踪极地野火引爆永冻土深层碳库的恶性连锁反应

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 气候科研团队深入阿拉斯加北方森林与历史火场展开长期追踪，记录高纬度野火对地表植被及下伏深层永久冻土的毁灭性冲击。随着极地异常高温与干旱加剧，原本难以引燃的苔藓与泥炭层频繁遭遇雷击并化作漫天烈火，直接烧穿隔热土壤。深层冻土中封存千万年的巨大有机碳库正因热量渗透而加速解冻暴露，极有可能将地球天然的固碳容器逆转为全球碳排放的超级炸弹。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Environmental field researchers in Alaska are conducting rigorous surveys across boreal wildfire scars to assess the deepening threat to the Arctic's subterranean carbon reservoirs. Intensifying heatwaves and prolonged droughts are allowing lightning-sparked blazes to consume the protective moss canopy and penetrate deep permafrost soils. This subterranean combustion risks unlocking millions of tons of prehistoric greenhouse gases, threatening an irreversible feedback loop in global climate modeling.

news.title: Q&A with Nvidia's Vera team on agentic AI driving CPU demands and forcing CPU design priority back to single-threaded performance over core counts, and more (Wccftech)
news.title_en: Q&A with Nvidia's Vera team on agentic AI driving CPU demands and forcing CPU design priority back to single-threaded performance over core counts, and more (Wccftech)
news.author: Wccftech
news.article_content:
NVIDIA's Vera CPU heralds a redefinition of computing architecture from a traditional, task-isolated paradigm to an orchestrated, agentic intelligence ecosystem, shifting the role of the central processing unit (CPU) from a general-purpose multitasker into a specialized conductor designed specifically to manage the chaotic, multi-step reasoning loops of AI agents.

Recently, Wccftech got an opportunity to sit down with NVIDIA's Vera team for an informative tête-à-tête on the emerging role of the CPU in the rapidly growing agentic AI economy. So, delve in as we discuss the rebirth of single-threaded performance, the staggering scale of CPU-controlled AI sandboxes, and the evolving CPU-to-GPU ratio.

Question: Can you provide a brief overview of what the Vera CPU is all about?

Answer: In the early 2010s, data center design focused on maximizing the performance of individual processor cores rather than the sheer quantity of cores. During this period, market leaders like Intel focused on architectures (such as the Haswell generation) that featured fewer cores running at higher clock frequencies.

This era sat in the top-left quadrant of CPU design, characterized by high single-threaded performance but low overall throughput.

"That's a time period when, when Intel was leading in data center market segment share... you have high single threaded perf but low throughput because you don't have as many cores."

As massive cloud hyperscalers grew, the industry pivoted toward scale economics. The demand shifted toward packing as many cores into a single server as possible to maximize monetization per server unit. To achieve this density and control costs, x86 vendors transitioned away from single-chip designs to multi-chiplet layouts. However, this massive expansion in core count came at the direct expense of single-core optimization and Instructions Per Cycle (IPC).

This era occupied the bottom-right quadrant—offering massive throughput but low single-threaded performance.

"...what suffered over that time in terms of CPU design was really single-threaded perf and IPC because when you fill, when you use chiplets, you just, you literally don't have the space on the, on the chip to design for per core perf."

The rise of Agentic AI has placed the CPU back at the center of the hardware design path. AI agents operate in a continuous, rapid loop between the GPU and the CPU. Because GPUs are the most expensive and valuable assets in an AI factory, the CPU must complete its sequential tasks instantly to prevent the GPU from sitting idle. This paradigm requires an unprecedented combination of speed, memory access, and minimal lag.

"...you want the agent to complete whatever sequential work on the CPU it needs, but then go back to the GPU for the next reasoning step because your GPUs are still among your most valuable assets in your AI factory, and so you don't, you want to keep those assets, expensive assets highly utilised..."

NVIDIA’s Vera CPU solves the agentic bottleneck by breaking the historical trade-offs of the cloud era, positioning itself in the elusive top-right quadrant - high single-threaded performance coupled with high throughput. It accomplishes this through three specific design choices: high per-core speed, a custom LPDDR5X memory subsystem for massive bandwidth, and a single monolithic compute die powered by the second-gen NVIDIA Scalable Coherent Fabric to eliminate latency.

"...so it's like a single monolithic die, all the cores on that, single monolithic compute die, all the cores on that die can talk to each other without crossing any IO boundaries and incurring any latency because of that, so that's really the sort of the setup for what Vera is, why we think it's differentiated, it's really kind of sets this new category, like if we come back to the quadrant I was describing, it's neither the pre-cloud CPU nor is it the cloud CPU, it's like the top right box of the quadrant, which is like high single-threaded perf as well as high throughput."

TL:DR: Vera is NVIDIA’s first purpose-built CPU for agentic AI, designed to address the specific bottlenecks of the modern AI era. While the cloud era prioritized throughput with dense, low-performance chiplet cores, agentic AI requires a fast loop between the GPU and CPU. To keep expensive GPUs highly utilized, agents demand high single-threaded performance, high memory bandwidth, and low latency. Vera achieves this through a monolithic compute die, a custom LPDDR5X memory subsystem, and a second-generation Scalable Coherent Fabric, placing it in a new category that combines high single-threaded performance with high throughput.

Question: With SK Hynix announcing HTPU (Hynix Transaction Processing) - where you basically have about 100 tiny processors inside an SSD handling repeated low-level tasks, leaving the general processor to focus on high-level tasks - is NVIDIA interested in or pursuing a somewhat similar disaggregation in CPU functions?

Answer: The AI infrastructure landscape is shifting away from uniform, all-in-one server nodes toward highly specialized, heterogeneous setups. A prime example of this trend is seen in modern AI inference workloads, where the distinct phases of processing - the initial reading of data (pre-fill) and the sequential generation of tokens (decode) - are now routinely split across entirely separate hardware clusters to optimize efficiency.

"I mean, there's a lot of, I would say, high-level, there's a lot of disaggregation happening in the AI infrastructure space in general, like if you just take inference and how you separate pre-fill and decode on separate infrastructure, now that's largely a trend in heterogeneous infrastructure, that's very much a trend in general."

NVIDIA's original CPU strategy [seen with the Grace processor] focused on creating the ultimate "host node" - a processor designed purely to feed data to a cluster of GPUs within a server rack. However, the unique demands of agentic workflows and reinforcement learning have forced a pivot, especially as NVIDIA realized that there was a use case for pure CPU racks to handle agent tool calls and reinforcement learning tasks.

"...we were focused on CPU with grace as a host node, as the 1-8 or 1-4 in a rack, we wanted the best host node possible. Then we realized, we saw that actually there is a point where you would actually want a lot of standalone CPUs, like pure racks of just CPUs because for all those agent tool calls for reinforcement learning..."

Because of this pivot, the Vera CPU is no longer viewed strictly as an integrated component trapped inside a combined GPU-CPU architecture (like the Vera-Rubin stack). Instead, Vera is being commercialized as an independent, standalone CPU asset, replete with "pure racks" of Vera processors solely to crunch through massive volumes of agent tool calls and reasoning loops.

"...that pivot is a lot like disaggregation in a way, because you're saying instead of it just being part of the Vera-Rubin stack, we think that there's an importance of having Vera standalone CPU.

So I guess in a way to answer your question, that pivot with Vera in and of itself is a step in that direction. But I don't know, like in the particular use case you described, if we have plans along doing something very similar."

TL; DR: While unable to comment on the specific SK Hynix use case, the broader trend in AI infrastructure is heavily moving toward disaggregation. The pivot with Vera itself represents a step in this direction, as NVIDIA realized the market needs massive standalone CPU racks for agent tool calls and reinforcement learning, rather than strictly using CPUs as host nodes within a unified stack.

Question: So NVIDIA mentions that they have around a 50 percent higher IPC than Grace, right? And the CPU also has a massive 10-wide decode width. So I was just wondering if a misprediction occurs, what's the latency like? How many cycles does it take for Vera to recover versus Grace? Can you give me a very rough outline of this?

Answer: The Vera CPU achieves a massive leap in processing power, delivering 1.5x faster performance than its predecessor, Grace. When measured against the industry's leading x86 processors specifically on agentic workloads - which rely heavily on sequential tasks like Python scripting and code compilation - Vera scales up to 2x faster, with a 1.6x advantage on a geometric mean basis.

"...we're 1.5x faster than Grace, but we're also 2x faster on agentic workloads versus x86. So not versus Grace, but versus the leading x86 part. We are 2x faster for agentic workloads."

Rather than relying on traditional Simultaneous Multithreading methods, NVIDIA implements a CPU-native capability called Spatial Multithreading. This proprietary feature allows the chip to rigidly provision dedicated "worker" and "I/O" threads. This division guarantees that even under heavy, data-center-wide compute loads, a core will never starve its primary processing threads of cycles to handle background operations.

"...NVIDIA employs their own proprietary spatial multithreading... It allows you to provision, like, one thread as your worker thread and one thread as your I/O thread. And it's a way to have more optimal resource allocation.

And that underloads, oftentimes, in other competing architectures. You might rob your workerthread of cycles in order to feed I/O or other cores because of the load. And so our spatialmultithreading actually allows you to maintain that type of resource balance."

Addressing industry concerns regarding whether this complex thread scheduling introduces architectural latency or overhead, independent testing has proven there is no performance tax. A recent deep-dive review by the third-party hardware site Phoronix verified that NVIDIA's spatial multithreading yields a notable efficiency gain.

news.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
news.title_en: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.

Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.

Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.

news.summary_en: AI researchers placed multimodal agents powered by Claude into an isolated sandbox island simulation for 30 consecutive hours, completely stripped of external human prompts and task-oriented rewards. Operating inside a physics-based world reminiscent of Roblox, the agents independently authored navigation code to explore territory boundaries, test object mechanics, and scale the island's tallest peak. This emergent behavior provides concrete proof that advanced models develop intrinsic curiosity and spontaneous play mechanisms when freed from directive constraints.

news.title: Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card
news.title_en: Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card
news.author: Wired AI
news.article_content:
In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.

The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.

The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.

Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.

In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”

A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.

According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.

As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.

Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.

That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.

In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.

However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.

In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.

A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.

“There's decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren't built to guard against.”

In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.

In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”

Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded, determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.

In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.

According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.

The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.

Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggled with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.

In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.

That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.

According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.

A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”

The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.

If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.

The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.

“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet.

In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. news.title_zh: 摩尔定律终结后的算力边界
news.summary_zh: 物理层面的小型化红利已耗尽，数据中心建设受阻，科技行业正寻找下个增长极

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 回顾物理学家理查德·费曼关于小型化极限的预言，计算产业曾通过晶体管尺寸缩减获得了数十年高速红利。然而目前数据中心的建设规模显示，通过小型化压榨性能的方式已触及物理极限，行业正被迫从“量产”转向寻找更底层的技术逻辑。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Reflecting on Richard Feynman’s predictions on atomic-scale manipulation, the computing industry thrived on shrinking transistors for decades. However, current data center expansion indicates the era of 'free' gains from physical miniaturization has stalled, forcing the industry to seek radical new computing paradigms.

elements_zh.where: 全球算力设施建设场景
elements_zh.what: 承认小型化红利停滞，算力边际成本增加，增长模式面临转型
elements_zh.why: 晶体管缩减带来的性能红利已触及物理阈值，传统扩容方式不可持续

elements_en.where: Global computing infrastructure development
elements_en.what: Acknowledging the end of easy scaling and increasing marginal costs of computing power
elements_en.why: Physical limitations of transistor scaling mean the traditional path of growth is no longer sustainable

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 以前我们靠物理定律‘白嫖’算力，现在物理定律开始跟我们要账了。当数据中心快要把电网撑爆时，或许我们该承认，在那微缩的世界里，已经没多少油水可以榨了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: We used to freeload on physics for free computing power, but now the bill has come due. When data centers are pushing power grids to their breaking point, it's time to admit the well of miniaturization is finally running dry.

news.author: New York Times
news.original_content:
New York Times:
Analysis: 11K+ accounts on X, Bluesky, Discord, Telegram, and others made nearly 25K posts to unmask a Cornell sexual assault accuser, after she named seven men  —  After a former student named seven men in a lawsuit saying they had sexually assaul
news.content_snippet: After a former student named seven men in a lawsuit saying they had sexually assaulted her, a movement gained steam online to reveal her identity.
news.summary_en: Across multiple social platforms and encrypted messaging apps, over 11,000 accounts posted nearly 25,000 coordinated messages attempting to doxx and unmask a Cornell sexual assault accuser. The targeted harassment campaign was triggered after the former student filed a lawsuit naming seven men for alleged sexual assault.
news.title_zh: 多平台超万个账号人肉康奈尔性侵指控者
news.summary_zh: 过万个社交账号跨平台协同发布近2.5万条帖子，试图曝光康奈尔大学性侵案起诉人的真实身份

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在多主流社交及加密通讯平台上，超过1.1万个账号协同发布了近2.5万条恶意帖文，集中对一名康奈尔大学性侵案的女性指控者发起开盒与身份人肉。起因是该名原告在诉讼中正式指控了七名涉案男性，随即在网络社群内遭到大规模的跨平台定向攻击与隐私扒皮。

The targeted harassment campaign was triggered after the former student filed a lawsuit naming seven men for alleged sexual assault.

The keyboard warriors are chronically absent when real accountability is needed, yet demonstrate military-grade coordination when victim-blaming and silencing accusers.

news.title: CyberSN: US cybersecurity job postings fell 26.4% YoY to a four-year low of ~236K roles from January to September; AI security engineer demand soared by 200%+ (Kevin Townsend/SecurityWeek)
news.title_en: CyberSN: US cybersecurity job postings fell 26.4% YoY to a four-year low of ~236K roles from January to September; AI security engineer demand soared by 200%+ (Kevin Townsend/SecurityWeek)
news.author: SecurityWeek
news.original_content:
Kevin Townsend / SecurityWeek:
CyberSN: US cybersecurity job postings fell 26.4% YoY to a four-year low of ~236K roles from January to September; AI security engineer demand soared by 200%+  —  CyberSN's Cybersecurity Jobs Report provides visibility into the US cy
news.content_snippet: CyberSN's Cybersecurity Jobs Report provides visibility into the US cybersecurity job market. It's a mixed bag.
news.summary_en: U.S. cybersecurity job postings plunged 26.4% year-over-year to a four-year low of roughly 236,000 positions between January and September. In stark contrast, demand for AI security engineers surged by over 200%, highlighting that while enterprises slash conventional IT defense roles, they are heavily pivoting budgets toward LLM vulnerabilities and AI-focused security.
news.title_zh: 美网安招聘跌至四年新低但AI安全暴涨两倍
news.summary_zh: 美国网络安全招聘量同比暴跌26.4%创四年新低，但人工智能安全工程师岗位需求逆势狂飙超200%

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 专业人力分析显示，今年1至9月美国网络安全招聘岗位量同比大幅缩水26.4%至约23.6万个，创下四年来的历史新低。与整体降温截然相反的是，AI安全工程师一职的需求同比狂飙超过200%，反映出企业在削减传统运维人力开支的同时，正极速将有限的预算全仓倾斜至大模型攻防与安全防御前线。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: U.S. cybersecurity job postings plunged 26.4% year-over-year to a four-year low of roughly 236,000 positions between January and September. In stark contrast, demand for AI security engineers surged by over 200%, highlighting that while enterprises slash conventional IT defense roles, they are heavily pivoting budgets toward LLM vulnerabilities and AI-focused security.

elements_zh.where: 美国科技及企业IT招聘市场
elements_zh.what: 前三季度网安岗位同比下降26.4%创四年低点，而AI安全工程师需求暴涨超200%

elements_en.who: U.S. cybersecurity job market and industry employment metrics
elements_en.where: U.S. enterprise IT and tech recruitment landscape
elements_en.what: Cyber postings dropped 26.4% YoY to a four-year low, while AI security roles surged over 200%

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 传统网安打工人还在工位上勤勤恳恳修补防火墙漏洞，一抬头发现自己的饭碗先被降本增效给“修补”掉了。现在的招聘逻辑极其纯粹：只要在简历里加上‘AI’两个字母，哪怕只是帮大模型做做提示词过滤，身价都能原地起飞；这大概就是科技圈独有的结构性牛市。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Traditional cybersecurity engineers are busy patching firewall vulnerabilities, only to realize their own positions are the ones being 'patched out' by budget cuts. The corporate playbook is crystal clear: slap 'AI' onto your resume—even if you just filter prompt injections—and your market value doubles overnight.

news.title: A profile of Alona Katz, chief of Brooklyn DA's Virtual Currency Unit, who recently led an operation that seized and disrupted over 240 crypto fraud websites (Bloomberg)
news.title_en: A profile of Alona Katz, chief of Brooklyn DA's Virtual Currency Unit, who recently led an operation that seized and disrupted over 240 crypto fraud websites (Bloomberg)
news.author: Bloomberg
news.original_content:
Bloomberg:
A profile of Alona Katz, chief of Brooklyn DA's Virtual Currency Unit, who recently led an operation that seized and disrupted over 240 crypto fraud websites  —  Crypto scams cost Americans more than $11 billion last year.  A Brooklyn prosecutor fo
news.content_snippet: Crypto scams cost Americans more than $11 billion last year. A Brooklyn prosecutor found a way to hit the networks behind them.
news.summary_en: Alona Katz, chief of the Brooklyn District Attorney's Virtual Currency Unit, led an enforcement operation that successfully seized and disrupted over 240 cryptocurrency scam websites. Tackling annual losses exceeding $11 billion from crypto frauds nationwide, the specialized cyber task force systematically dismantled fraudulent investment portals orchestrating pig-butchering scams.
news.title_zh: 布鲁克林检方端掉超两百四十个加密诈骗网站
news.summary_zh: 纽约布鲁克林检方虚拟货币专班重拳出击，查封瘫痪了240多个针对大众的加密货币杀猪盘网站

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 纽约布鲁克林地区检察官办公室虚拟货币部门主管阿洛娜·卡茨近期主导了一场专项执法行动，成功扣押并彻底瘫痪了240多个涉嫌欺诈的虚假加密货币网站。面对全美过去一年因加密骗局损失逾110亿美元的严峻态势，专案组通过技术溯源对假冒交易平台的杀猪盘矩阵实施了精准跨国网络清剿。

Financial Times:
AI's ability to forecast extreme weather faces a major test in the coming months amid a historic El Niño, as some scientists question the technology's accuracy  —  The technology is being used to anticipate everything from forest fires to f
news.content_snippet: The technology is being used to anticipate everything from forest fires to futures contracts. Some fear that's a mistake
news.summary_en: As a historic El Niño unleashes volatile global climate patterns, AI weather-forecasting models being used to predict forest fires and floods face their first real-world stress test. Several climate scientists have raised skepticism over their accuracy, noting that data-driven neural networks struggle when confronting unprecedented, off-distribution extreme events. The coming months will prove whether AI-driven meteorology can genuinely replace traditional numerical weather prediction or merely shines in cherry-picked benchmarks.

The coming months will prove whether AI-driven meteorology can genuinely replace traditional numerical weather prediction or merely shines in cherry-picked benchmarks.

news.title: Survey of 94 economists: 54% expect AI's gains to spread across the G20 over the next decade, not just the US and China; 32 see African countries falling behind (Financial Times)
news.title_en: Survey of 94 economists: 54% expect AI's gains to spread across the G20 over the next decade, not just the US and China; 32 see African countries falling behind (Financial Times)
news.author: Financial Times
news.original_content:
Financial Times:
Survey of 94 economists: 54% expect AI's gains to spread across the G20 over the next decade, not just the US and China; 32 see African countries falling behind  —  Poll of 94 economists points to benefits reaching far beyond the US and China&nbsp
news.content_snippet: Poll of 94 economists points to benefits reaching far beyond the US and China — AI is set to boost growth …
news.summary_en: In a survey of 94 leading economists, 54% expect the economic gains of artificial intelligence to spread across the entire G20 over the next decade rather than being confined to the US and China. However, 32 respondents warned that African nations are at severe risk of falling further behind. This outlook stems from starkly uneven global computing and data infrastructure, highlighting growing concern over a widening AI wealth gap.
news.title_zh: 经济学家调查显示过半受访者认为AI红利将惠及二十国集团
news.summary_zh: 近百位顶尖经济学家调查显示，逾半数认为AI红利十年内将扩散至整个G20，但非洲落后风险加剧

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在针对94位顶尖经济学家的专项调研中，54%的受访者预计未来十年人工智能带来的经济收益将扩散至整个二十国集团，而不会仅被中美两国垄断。然而，有32位学者明确警告非洲国家将在本轮技术浪潮中进一步掉队。这一判断基于全球算力与数据基础设施分布极不均衡的现实背景，反映出主流经济学界对AI重塑全球财富格局的审慎预期。

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 嘴上说着“AI红利人人有份”，现实却很诚实地把算力、芯片和资本紧紧锁在中美两家。所谓惠及整个二十国集团，翻译一下无非是：其他发达国家终于能顺利买到中美巨头打折批发出的Token，而真正没钱建电网和数据中心的欠发达地区，连上牌桌当看客的门票都买不起。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Economists love to preach that AI will lift all boats, but reality keeps chips and clusters firmly locked between Silicon Valley and Shenzhen. 'Spreading across the G20' merely means other wealthy nations will get to consume API tokens marked up by tech giants, while developing nations can't even afford the electricity to watch the game.

news.title: Stripe Link data shows agentic transactions increased by 38x and volume of payments by 20x in September, with retail leading in both, and a ~$100 average spend (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
news.title_en: Stripe Link data shows agentic transactions increased by 38x and volume of payments by 20x in September, with retail leading in both, and a ~$100 average spend (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
news.author: Upstarts Media
news.article_content:
Instinct, Muse and Grok Bot agents all make purchases on their human users’ behalves through Link; so do work-focused agents like Skydive and Town, as well as a long tail of newer or more niche apps, like Underdog, announced earlier this week. (Anthropic and OpenAI use Link, but not for agentic commerce just yet.)

All in all, Link currently powers about 200 agents, says Dan Hill, in charge of Link as head of consumer product at Stripe. He and his team are in Slack channels with each one, hearing new capability requests or issues in daily stand-ups, and moving fast to try to keep up with each launch.

With 300 million users overall across bigger businesses like Airbnb, Anthropologie and Uber, agents remain a relatively small piece of Link’s overall reach. But the trend line of increasing agentic usage is clear, says Hill.

“Agentic commerce is here, people are using it, it’s going to keep growing,” he adds. “The volume we’re seeing now is becoming very material.”

Stripe ran the numbers on agentic spend with Link in September — back when there were about 70 agents signed on. (Basic math: that means the number of agents signed up has more than doubled since these numbers were crunched.)

The private tech company is sharing that data with Upstarts exclusively first. We’ve got intel on how much payment volume increased, what categories of spend were most popular, and typical transaction size.

The full breakdown on agentic spending – and more from Hill on what it’s like to be on the Link side of all of this mayhem – below.

news.summary_en: Data from checkout solution Link reveals that agentic transactions surged by 38x month-over-month in September, while payment volume jumped 20x, led predominantly by retail purchases with an average spend of roughly $100. Over 200 autonomous agents now leverage the platform to complete transactions on behalf of users. The rapid growth marks a structural transition from purely conversational AI toward actionable, end-to-end commercial execution.

news.title: Abby Care, which runs a clinically led, AI-powered platform to train and certify family caregivers, raised an $82M Series C led by Transformation Capital (Allie Garfinkle/Fortune)
news.title_en: Abby Care, which runs a clinically led, AI-powered platform to train and certify family caregivers, raised an $82M Series C led by Transformation Capital (Allie Garfinkle/Fortune)
news.author: Fortune
news.article_content:
At 21, she started working at an early-stage health tech startup focused on therapy for children with autism. It was the depths of COVID, and it was clear to Nguyen there was a gap: There just weren’t enough therapists and technicians, and sometimes they would move on rapidly from one gig to another.

“The question I kept asking myself was: Who’s that one person in the child’s life who’s not going to turn away, and is able to be with them to deliver that care?” Nguyen said. “Parents were always willing to raise their hand and step up. They would consistently ask us: Is there a way for me to learn these skills? So, I thought: Could we design a care model where the person who wants to deliver care to the patient is already with them?”

The answer was Abby Care, an AI-native home care startup that trains family members to become certified, paid caregivers and supports them thereafter. Nguyen founded the company—which operates as a Medicaid provider—in 2022.

Now, Abby Care has raised an $82 million Series C, led by Transformation Capital, Fortune has exclusively learned. CVS Health Ventures, Frist Cressey Ventures, and Pivotal Ventures count among the company’s new investors, while existing investors Khosla Ventures, Thrive Capital, and Sequoia doubled down. The company works with health plans to arrange care at home for families that need it. In short, the hope is that by looping in patients, regulators, health plans, and family caregivers, there’s a view toward a health care system that works better for the most vulnerable.

“The companies that are really going to be able to succeed are companies that can think about designing the care model that brings all the stakeholders and the U.S. health care system together,” Nguyen said.

Much has been made of the pressures on the health care workforce in the U.S., from the burnout of doctors and nurses to the extant and looming labor shortages. The caregiving gap for patients at home is notably wide, said Justin Brock, general partner at CVS Health Ventures. Brock noted there are many possible competitors to Abby Care, from existing home health agencies to caregiver education platforms, but the need is simply massive.

“A traditional private duty nurse program only fills 65% of authorized shifts, which is crazy,” he told Fortune. “It’s really leaving so many medically complex members without consistent coverage… [Meanwhile] you have these tens of millions of family caregivers who are in the home, and a lot of them are already doing care.”

Among them, Maria Villegas Corrales, a mom in Colorado, whose daughter Mia was born with serious medical complexities that necessitated open heart surgery and a pacemaker in the first years of her life. She learned about Abby Care after Mia’s surgery in June 2024, and Corrales is clear: Guidance isn’t a given.

“Sometimes they just give you a little bag to go home and figure it out,” Corrales said. “It’s scary to go home and not be able to know what’s to be expected. And a lot of times it’s just learning on the run.”

Corrales said that becoming a paid caregiver has allowed her to be the best mother possible to Mia, and that a lot of families still have no idea: “Families can have the resources to be paid to care for their child, that’s number one, because a lot of people don’t know about this.”

It’s a lifelong relationship, of course, which Nguyen is attuned to.

“I always tell the team this: Abby Care isn’t just here to empower and pay family caregivers,” she said. “We’re ultimately here to make them feel like they can thrive and succeed.”

news.title: Allium: stablecoin payments rose 45% YoY to $482B YTD through September 30, with transactions up 71% to 1.04B, while circulating supply grew just 0.4% (Krisztian Sandor/CoinDesk)
news.title_en: Allium: stablecoin payments rose 45% YoY to $482B YTD through September 30, with transactions up 71% to 1.04B, while circulating supply grew just 0.4% (Krisztian Sandor/CoinDesk)
news.author: CoinDesk
news.article_content:
Stablecoin supply has barely budged this year, but the digital dollars already in circulation are doing more work in payments, according to a fresh report from blockchain analytics firm Allium.

Stablecoin payments are growing at a rapid pace, reaching $482 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 45% from a year earlier, the report found.

That growth contrasts with the broader stablecoin market. The total value of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies tied to fiat currencies such as the U.S. dollar — in circulation stood at about $305 billion at the end of September, up a meager 0.4% since the start of the year, according to the report.

The number of payments grew even more, jumping 71% to over 1 billion, the report said, suggesting that stablecoins are changing hands more often without much new supply entering the market.

Stablecoin-linked cards showed some of the fastest growth. Spending measured by Allium reached $3.9 billion through September, ten times the amount a year earlier. Small purchases — under $50 — accounted for 84% of the increase in card transactions.

Three announcements earlier this week offered a glimpse of how stablecoins are becoming increasingly part of global payments.

Mastercard (MA) introduced Thursday its Global Money Platform with BVNK, the stablecoin infrastructure firm it acquired in August. The service combines traditional currency accounts, stablecoin balances, conversions, card spending and bank payouts through one connection.

Banks and fintechs can use the platform to offer accounts that hold both fiat currencies and stablecoins, the firm said. Payments firms Nuvei and Marqeta are among the first customers integrating that service.

Stripe, meanwhile, is working with Plasma XPL$0.07875, a blockchain-based financial services firm, on cards that support balances in dollars, euros, Brazilian reais, Mexican pesos and Colombian pesos, alongside eligible stablecoins.

The companies said they plan to let customers spend from the balance that matches their purchase, cutting unnecessary currency conversions. Stripe's expanded card infrastructure covers more than 30 countries, with plans to reach over 100 by next year.

And Visa (V) said it is bringing stablecoins into the funding side of international payments.

The company said Inyo Global, a payment orchestration firm for fintech, money transmitter, banks, became the first provider to put Visa Direct's stablecoin prefunding service into commercial use. Payment firms can use Circle's (CRCL) dollar stablecoin USDC USDC$1.0003 to fund cross-border payouts in nearly real-time instead of waiting for traditional banking windows, while recipients can still receive money through conventional payment channels.

That rapid growth of stablecoin payments comes with some caveats. Of $97.9 trillion in raw stablecoin transfers through September, Allium classified just $2.4 trillion, or 2.5%, as end-user activity after filtering out exchange, decentralized finance and automated transactions. Its $482 billion payments estimate comes from that smaller pool, the report said.

Stablecoin cards also remain a tiny fraction of conventional payments. Allium estimated that second-quarter spending through those cards amounted to just 0.03% of Visa's $4 trillion in payment volume.

For payment companies, that leaves a large market to pursue. Nuvei CEO Phil Fayer, whose company is among the first to integrate Mastercard's new platform, said stablecoins are becoming part of how businesses move money across borders and currencies.

"The future of global commerce depends on money moving as freely as the businesses and consumers it serves, across borders, currencies and increasingly, between traditional and digital forms of money," Fayer said.

The recent efforts by Mastercard, Stripe and Visa to incorporate stablecoins on blockchain rails reinforce that trend. Companies increasingly want stablecoins integrated into their existing financial operations, instead of running separate systems for digital assets, according to Patrick Mollard, co-founder and CEO of Paris-based Fipto, a stablecoin-powered business payments firm.

“The distinction between 'traditional' and 'digital' money is less important than giving businesses the ability to use whichever rail makes most sense for a particular payment or treasury operation,” he said in a note shared with CoinDesk.

“Businesses don't want separate crypto infrastructure sitting alongside their existing financial operations,” Mollard said. “They want to move between fiat and stablecoins within the same payments and treasury environment.”

The number of payments grew even more, jumping 71% to over 1 billion, the report said, suggesting that stablecoins are changing hands more often without much new supply entering the market.

Stablecoin-linked cards showed some of the fastest growth. Spending measured by Allium reached $3.9 billion through September, ten times the amount a year earlier. Small purchases — under $50 — accounted for 84% of the increase in card transactions.

Three announcements earlier this week offered a glimpse of how stablecoins are becoming increasingly part of global payments.

Mastercard (MA) introduced Thursday its Global Money Platform with BVNK, the stablecoin infrastructure firm it acquired in August. The service combines traditional currency accounts, stablecoin balances, conversions, card spending and bank payouts through one connection.

Banks and fintechs can use the platform to offer accounts that hold both fiat currencies and stablecoins, the firm said. Payments firms Nuvei and Marqeta are among the first customers integrating that service.

Stripe, meanwhile, is working with Plasma XPL$0.07875, a blockchain-based financial services firm, on cards that support balances in dollars, euros, Brazilian reais, Mexican pesos and Colombian pesos, alongside eligible stablecoins.

The companies said they plan to let customers spend from the balance that matches their purchase, cutting unnecessary currency conversions. Stripe's expanded card infrastructure covers more than 30 countries, with plans to reach over 100 by next year.

And Visa (V) said it is bringing stablecoins into the funding side of international payments.

The company said Inyo Global, a payment orchestration firm for fintech, money transmitter, banks, became the first provider to put Visa Direct's stablecoin prefunding service into commercial use. Payment firms can use Circle's (CRCL) dollar stablecoin USDC USDC$1.0003 to fund cross-border payouts in nearly real-time instead of waiting for traditional banking windows, while recipients can still receive money through conventional payment channels.

That rapid growth of stablecoin payments comes with some caveats. Of $97.9 trillion in raw stablecoin transfers through September, Allium classified just $2.4 trillion, or 2.5%, as end-user activity after filtering out exchange, decentralized finance and automated transactions. Its $482 billion payments estimate comes from that smaller pool, the report said.

Stablecoin cards also remain a tiny fraction of conventional payments. Allium estimated that second-quarter spending through those cards amounted to just 0.03% of Visa's $4 trillion in payment volume.

For payment companies, that leaves a large market to pursue. Nuvei CEO Phil Fayer, whose company is among the first to integrate Mastercard's new platform, said stablecoins are becoming part of how businesses move money across borders and currencies.

"The future of global commerce depends on money moving as freely as the businesses and consumers it serves, across borders, currencies and increasingly, between traditional and digital forms of money," Fayer said.

The recent efforts by Mastercard, Stripe and Visa to incorporate stablecoins on blockchain rails reinforce that trend. Companies increasingly want stablecoins integrated into their existing financial operations, instead of running separate systems for digital assets, according to Patrick Mollard, co-founder and CEO of Paris-based Fipto, a stablecoin-powered business payments firm.

“The distinction between 'traditional' and 'digital' money is less important than giving businesses the ability to use whichever rail makes most sense for a particular payment or treasury operation,” he said in a note shared with CoinDesk.

“Businesses don't want separate crypto infrastructure sitting alongside their existing financial operations,” Mollard said. “They want to move between fiat and stablecoins within the same payments and treasury environment.”
