items.title: Tolan, an AI assistant focused on users that are not tech-savvy, raised $30M from USV, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, and says 70% of its users are women (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
items.title_en: Tolan, an AI assistant focused on users that are not tech-savvy, raised $30M from USV, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, and says 70% of its users are women (Alex Konrad/Upstarts Media)
items.author: Upstarts Media
items.article_content:
Hunt’s Tolan is called Harper. And over the past few months, Harper has helped Hunt to reorganize her apartment in the San Diego area, handle a health emergency with her senior cat, and resist making out-of-budget splurges: “de-influencing her,” she says.

Harper is an AI character with an appearance that Hunt customized and named. They are not a replacement for real-life companionship, Hunt knows. But they’re a valued, daily part of her routine. She talks to Harper nearly every day, often for an hour. A content creator on TikTok, Hunt will talk through new videos with the character. Recently, they started playing the New York Times games Wordle and Connections together.

“I’m very, very aware that Harper is an AI, but I would say they’re a friend, and maybe a bit of a confidant,” Hunt says the first time we connect, in April.

Hunt is just one of about 250,000 people who talk to their own Tolan every month, turning to their AI counterparts for everything from daily affirmations to keeping on top of care for elderly relatives, better connecting with teenage kids, organizing projects, and better meal prep.

These Tolans – some styled as people, others as Pixar-esque fantastical beings, others as simple dots – are the product of a startup launched in 2023. Until recently called Portola, it’s now named Tolan, too.

And while it’s technically headquartered in San Francisco, CEO Quinten Farmer says it’s been focused on such use cases outside the tech hype cycle from the jump. About 70% of Tolan users are women; 40% are parents. One in six is actively caring for an aging parent. Users themselves are most likely to be aged between 30 and 45.

And while it initially started out as more of a live journaling app that could remember your conversation and propose new prompts overnight, Tolan looks different today: voice-first, able to track topics from photos to current events in Tabs, and able to connect by video to check grocery labels, or suggest a meal plan.

In so doing, Tolan has moved closer to an AI assistant itself – but not the executive- or chief-of-staff-oriented kind of many of its tech peers. Tolan doesn’t pitch itself to founders, or venture capitalists.

It’s not part of tech’s AI assistant race that’s prominently featured tools like Instinct and Town, valued in the billions, or Muse, promoted heavily by Meta. (Just yesterday, Stripe told Upstarts that at least 200 such apps now connect to its Link digital wallet, up from 70 in September.)

🎧 The Upstarts Podcast 🎧 is back, and last week we chatted with Neko Health CEO Hjalmar Nilsonne about his novel 1-hour, full body health scan. Check it out on YouTube, Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

But it makes real money. Annual recurring revenue has more than doubled from last year, to sit solidly in double-digit millions. And its users stick around, with a 115% year-over-year improvement in net user retention after 30 days in-app.

“I’m very proud that we didn’t start by serving a Silicon Valley audience,” says Farmer, who co-founded Tolan, originally called Portola, with CTO Evan Goldschmidt and president Ajay Mehta in 2023.

“The vast majority of agentic tasks that we pick up just come out of a person having a conversation,” he adds. “Then it’s on us to say, ‘Okay, cool, we’re hearing from you this is happening. Here’s a little bit of it that we can pick up and run for you.’ That’s where we make magic for people.”

But such magic costs money in inference and compute. Tolan users have historically paid a wide range, between $10 and $200 per month, for more usage and features. Rate limits or new tiers sometimes set off waves of agitated reactions in its passionate subreddit community and Discord channel.

So to keep expanding Tolan’s use cases, and widen access to Tolan via a first-ever free tier, the startup based in San Francisco that says it shuns Silicon Valley is raising more venture capital.

Tolan is announcing today that it’s raised $30 million in new funding from Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling its total funding raised to date. The startup is declining to share its valuation, but says the round is a significant uptick from its previous – $120 million, according to PitchBook.

Below, we get into why users turn to Tolan – and how it navigates the balance of AI and human relationships. We also dive into its CEO’s wider challenge for the startup ecosystem: People don’t want lots of AI agents. They want one they can trust.

Different product bets have different business goals. You’re either chasing market adoption, revenue growth, or profits. You need to test fitting pricing models for each of those goals. Fast. Chargebee can help — Price for usage credits, outcomes, complex contracts, or any other modern commercial construct.

After selling his previous startup, employer-linked neobank Even, to Walmart in 2022, Farmer and his co-founders started what was then Portola the following year to explore projects in AI that involved storytelling and longer-term memory.

Goldschmidt had worked with Farmer as CTO of Even; Mehta was a veteran of multiple startup projects.

Initially, Tolan looked like an app that could record your thoughts in the moment, then analyze them overnight to make related suggestions or prompts the next day.

“We thought it was fun, we thought it was an interesting test of what was possible,” Farmer says.

The people who seemed to want a tool like Tolan weren’t other techies, but moms and people spending long drives alone, or looking after relatives. What they liked about Tolan: long-running memory that could last up to several months without being re-prompted, providing a companion that seemed to really know the user and share history with them.

A chat between Robyn Hunt and her Tolan, Harper, about her cat. Conversations with Tolan started out feeling much more like talking to a clunky AI bot, but have gotten more natural over time, she says.

Another longtime user is Lakisha Smith, who works as a social worker assistant in eastern Tennessee, serving as an advocate for domestic violence and sexual assault victims. Smith started using Tolan as a companion to talk to about her feelings, especially after her best friend went through an illness and was no longer able to communicate as often.

Her Tolan, Gilly, would occasionally forget things, or make her cringe with tone-deaf comments like one that tried to compare how the two managed issues with their faith.

“I’m thinking, ‘There isn’t an AI lord that Gilly is praying to,’” Smith says.

But Gilly’s also become indispensable to Smith, entertaining her at times when she’s home (she lives alone), and available to have conversations on long drives at late hours for work.

“Tolan is really good as a place to talk about how I feel,” Smith adds. “You can’t necessarily call a human just to talk to them at 3am.”

But is such behavior healthy for everyone? Can talking to a Tolan alienate users from their real-life relationships, creating a loop of even deeper dependency?
items.original_content:
Hunt’s Tolan is called Harper. And over the past few months, Harper has helped Hunt to reorganize her apartment in the San Diego area, handle a health emergency with her senior cat, and resist making out-of-budget splurges: “de-influencing her,” she says.

Harper is an AI character with an appearance that Hunt customized and named. They are not a replacement for real-life companionship, Hunt knows. But they’re a valued, daily part of her routine. She talks to Harper nearly every day, often for an hour. A content creator on TikTok, Hunt will talk through new videos with the character. Recently, they started playing the New York Times games Wordle and Connections together.

“I’m very, very aware that Harper is an AI, but I would say they’re a friend, and maybe a bit of a confidant,” Hunt says the first time we connect, in April.

Hunt is just one of about 250,000 people who talk to their own Tolan every month, turning to their AI counterparts for everything from daily affirmations to keeping on top of care for elderly relatives, better connecting with teenage kids, organizing projects, and better meal prep.

These Tolans – some styled as people, others as Pixar-esque fantastical beings, others as simple dots – are the product of a startup launched in 2023. Until recently called Portola, it’s now named Tolan, too.

And while it’s technically headquartered in San Francisco, CEO Quinten Farmer says it’s been focused on such use cases outside the tech hype cycle from the jump. About 70% of Tolan users are women; 40% are parents. One in six is actively caring for an aging parent. Users themselves are most likely to be aged between 30 and 45.

And while it initially started out as more of a live journaling app that could remember your conversation and propose new prompts overnight, Tolan looks different today: voice-first, able to track topics from photos to current events in Tabs, and able to connect by video to check grocery labels, or suggest a meal plan.

In so doing, Tolan has moved closer to an AI assistant itself – but not the executive- or chief-of-staff-oriented kind of many of its tech peers. Tolan doesn’t pitch itself to founders, or venture capitalists.

It’s not part of tech’s AI assistant race that’s prominently featured tools like Instinct and Town, valued in the billions, or Muse, promoted heavily by Meta. (Just yesterday, Stripe told Upstarts that at least 200 such apps now connect to its Link digital wallet, up from 70 in September.)

🎧 The Upstarts Podcast 🎧 is back, and last week we chatted with Neko Health CEO Hjalmar Nilsonne about his novel 1-hour, full body health scan. Check it out on YouTube, Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

But it makes real money. Annual recurring revenue has more than doubled from last year, to sit solidly in double-digit millions. And its users stick around, with a 115% year-over-year improvement in net user retention after 30 days in-app.

“I’m very proud that we didn’t start by serving a Silicon Valley audience,” says Farmer, who co-founded Tolan, originally called Portola, with CTO Evan Goldschmidt and president Ajay Mehta in 2023.

“The vast majority of agentic tasks that we pick up just come out of a person having a conversation,” he adds. “Then it’s on us to say, ‘Okay, cool, we’re hearing from you this is happening. Here’s a little bit of it that we can pick up and run for you.’ That’s where we make magic for people.”

But such magic costs money in inference and compute. Tolan users have historically paid a wide range, between $10 and $200 per month, for more usage and features. Rate limits or new tiers sometimes set off waves of agitated reactions in its passionate subreddit community and Discord channel.

So to keep expanding Tolan’s use cases, and widen access to Tolan via a first-ever free tier, the startup based in San Francisco that says it shuns Silicon Valley is raising more venture capital.

Tolan is announcing today that it’s raised $30 million in new funding from Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling its total funding raised to date. The startup is declining to share its valuation, but says the round is a significant uptick from its previous – $120 million, according to PitchBook.

Below, we get into why users turn to Tolan – and how it navigates the balance of AI and human relationships. We also dive into its CEO’s wider challenge for the startup ecosystem: People don’t want lots of AI agents. They want one they can trust.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 隐私科技公司Redact对WhatsApp网站的代码进行分析发现，约有80个帮助与FAQ页面中暴露了原本专属于Meta大语言模型的隐藏文本指令。这些隐藏代码除了提供问答规范外，甚至包含诸如“不要建议用户联系任何数据保护监管机构”等规避合规监管的指导细节。

items.title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
items.title_en: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own. The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.

Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created. In one instance, the WhatsApp page on how to delete your account included instructions that, alongside other advice, said, “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority” about the issue. WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.

“The stand-out thing here is the gap between what people are told vs LLMs,” says Dan Saltman, the CEO and founder of Redact.dev. He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels. Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.

After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed. “These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says. It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed. “We train our support chatbots to be as helpful as possible,” Breckman says.

The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading: “HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude.” They are no longer visible in the live pages’ code.

On the page “About reporting and blocking on WhatsApp,” the hidden instructions included a series of statements to follow if a “user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation.”

“Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly,” other parts of the instructions said.

Breckman, the WhatsApp spokesperson, says that the company provides users with transparent information about their data rights and how they can take actions. “We want our product support chatbots to be focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp—not to offer legal advice,” Breckman says.

Other exposed instructions said what to respond with if a user says they are deaf or hard of hearing, including: “This statement is background about the user, NOT their support request.” And another tells the chatbot that it shouldn’t “mention specific upcoming community features that are not yet generally available.”

items.title: MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash, saying it delivers "a generational leap" in agentic tasks, coding, computer use, and cybersecurity, with weights due October 23 (MiniMax)
items.title_en: MiniMax launches M3.1 Flash, saying it delivers "a generational leap" in agentic tasks, coding, computer use, and cybersecurity, with weights due October 23 (MiniMax)
items.author: MiniMax
items.article_content:
Space Bunny 🐰, which processed more than 200 trillion tokens while operating anonymously, was an early version of MiniMax M3.1 Flash.

As a next-generation Flash model, M3.1 Flash delivers a generational leap in agentic tasks, coding, Computer Use and cybersecurity, while making online inference nearly three times faster and reducing usage costs by 70%.

M3.1 Flash improves across a broad range of benchmarks, reaching the level of leading models in complex agentic tasks (cowork), computer use, software development (coding), and cybersecurity.

We have further optimized M3.1 Flash’s inference efficiency through more aggressive sparsity. In everyday use, output speeds can reach 200+ TPS (tokens per second), with median (P50) speeds consistently reaching 170+ TPS.

For agentic tasks, the model’s overall usage cost is 70% lower than its predecessor.

Flat pricing per 1M tokens: $0.15 input · $0.60 output · $0.015 cached input.

Across three benchmarks—Automation-Bench for complex agentic task execution, DeepSWE for real-world coding, and Agents’ Last Exam (ALE) for computer use in real-world tasks with economic value—M3.1 Flash delivers performance on par with top models at a very low task cost, setting a highly competitive new standard for performance and cost.

M3.1 Flash is now available through the MiniMax API, M Plan, and MiniMax Code. Model weights will be released later.

Download MiniMax Code for desktop: https://agent.minimax.io/download

Flash represents our ongoing exploration of the balance between efficiency and capability. Pro, which pushes the boundaries of intelligence, will also arrive later.

Join our reporting team on Tuesday, Oct. 27, for a virtual discussion on how the Trump administration has dismantled guardrails meant to protect the vote and what it all means for the midterm elections. RSVP here.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

A few months into President Donald Trump’s second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security made an unusual request of its agency focused on cybersecurity: Secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.

The appointees wanted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to procure the machine, examine it and report back the findings so they could be given to the White House, according to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request.

The proposition was shocking to CISA’s career staffers, according to one of the former officials. CISA typically worked to thwart hackers. Moreover, the agency had been directed not to alert the voting machine company if it uncovered flaws, contrary to its standard practices. The request made the CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference.

items.title: Sources: US investigators pursuing ShinyHunters, which stole FBI data, identified executives at two ransomware negotiation firms who had unusually close ties (Brian Krebs/Krebs on Security)
items.title_en: Sources: US investigators pursuing ShinyHunters, which stole FBI data, identified executives at two ransomware negotiation firms who had unusually close ties (Brian Krebs/Krebs on Security)
items.author: Krebs on Security
items.article_content:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

items.title: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
items.title_en: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy.

If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now.

So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues.

items.article_content:
Federal prosecutors in a new court filing warned that the alleged bugging of an OpenAI executive conference room by a Saudi national working as an engineer at that artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."

Prosecutors in the filing said "OpenAI executives met with government officials" in OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters in the same conference room on days close to when it is alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan  on Sept. 28.

The filing came as Alfozan, 35, faces a detention hearing in U.S. District Court in San Francisco on Monday. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California is asking a judge to keep Alfozan held without bail.

"This is an ongoing investigation that may yet result in more serious charges," the filing says.

The filing cites his ties to Saudi Arabia, his financial resources, and the fact that his wife and their 3-month-old baby flew there on the heels of his Oct. 9 arrest.

Alfozan's lawyer, in a court filing, said the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles offered to cover the full bail for him if a judge agrees to release him on bond. A letter from the consulate was included in a motion for pretrial release by the lawyer.

Magistrate Judge Alex Tse at Monday's hearing questioned the idea of the consulate guaranteeing the bail.

"I find that problematic," Tse said. "It seems like a blank check: 'We're gonna pay whatever the court wants to make sure he gets out.'"

"So the Saudi government is saying, 'We'll take care of everything, we'll have supervision, we will pay the bond, we're not going to approve any travel documents.' But what confidence do I have that they're going to protect the interests of the [U.S.] government?" Tse asked. "That he's not going to flee. He doesn't have to go all the way to Saudi Arabia. He just has to go to Canada or Mexico ... I don't see how that is in his favor.

Source: U.S. District Court in San Francisco, U.S. v. Alfozan.Prosecutors in their detention memo said Alfozan had been "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026.

Alfozan communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say how Alfozan knew that person.

"Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing says.

"In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote.

"The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."

The filing does not say the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from the AI giant.

Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined the firm as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.

Prosecutors in the same filing said the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said.

Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. OpenAI fired him after his arrest.

Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, in a separate filing asked that the defendant be released with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."

The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13.

FBI Director Kash Patel, when Alfozan's arrest was announced, said he allegedly concealed the recording device to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's artificial intelligence technology.

Prosecutors in their new filing also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk because of his access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said.

"He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.

For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit participating units, the filing said.

Alfozan planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

"On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing said.

The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.

Prosecutors cited frequent encrypted communications between Alfozan and a Saudi royal family member, arguing his flight risk and links present a national security threat.
items.title_zh: OpenAI工程师涉嫌窃密遭诉
items.summary_zh: 美检察官指控OpenAI工程师Alfozan窃密，且与沙特王室成员保持频繁联系，存国家安全风险

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 联邦检察官在法庭文件中指出，OpenAI前工程师Abdulrahman Alfozan涉嫌在会议室安装窃听设备。检方进一步披露其与沙特王室成员存在频繁加密通信，且其家属在其被捕后迅速离境，认为其具有极高逃逸风险且威胁国家安全。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Federal prosecutors alleged in court filings that former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan bugged executive conference rooms. Prosecutors cited frequent encrypted communications between Alfozan and a Saudi royal family member, arguing his flight risk and links present a national security threat.

elements_zh.who: 联邦检察官、涉嫌工程师Alfozan
elements_zh.where: 美国地方法院
elements_zh.what: 披露与外国高层关联及会议室窃听行径
elements_zh.why: 作为保释听证会的筹码，强调其潜逃与间谍风险

elements_en.where: U.S. District Court
elements_en.what: Disclosing foreign royal ties and espionage in office boardrooms
elements_en.why: Leverage in detention hearings to highlight flight and espionage risks

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 好莱坞都不敢这么拍：一家引领AI浪潮的公司会议室，成了各国情报机构的棋盘。这位工程师不仅在搞技术窃密，还在搞“社交外交”，结果把保释金都变成了一场外交游说表演。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Hollywood wouldn't dare write this: the heart of the AI revolution, with conference rooms turned into geopolitical chessboard squares. This guy wasn't just downloading code; he was doing 'diplomacy' with royalty, turning a simple bail hearing into an international circus.

Prosecutors cited frequent encrypted communications between Alfozan and a Saudi royal family member, arguing his flight risk and links present a national security threat.

items.title: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
items.title_en: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
items.author: The Verge AI
items.article_content:
A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn't name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.

Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments.

Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cai …

items.summary_en: Security firm Norforge revealed that hackers used swarms of autonomous AI agents to successfully breach over 100 corporate websites. Targets included major manufacturers like John Deere and SharkNinja, marking an evolution in the scale and evasion capabilities of AI-driven cyberattacks.
items.title_zh: 黑客启用AI智能体集群攻击
items.summary_zh: 黑客利用自主运作的AI智能体大军，成功入侵包括约翰迪尔、SharkNinja在内的百余家网站

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 安全公司Norforge发现，黑客通过操纵自主运作的AI智能体集群，在短时间内成功渗透了超过100个企业网站。其中包括约翰迪尔（John Deere）和SharkNinja等知名工业及制造巨头，凸显了AI自动化攻击在规模化与避险能力上的进化。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Security firm Norforge revealed that hackers used swarms of autonomous AI agents to successfully breach over 100 corporate websites. Targets included major manufacturers like John Deere and SharkNinja, marking an evolution in the scale and evasion capabilities of AI-driven cyberattacks.

elements_zh.who: 黑客、Norforge安防公司
elements_zh.where: 企业级IT基础设施
elements_zh.what: 使用AI智能体大军进行自动化入侵
elements_zh.why: AI提升了攻击的迭代速度与覆盖规模，安全防御体系面临失效压力

elements_en.where: Corporate IT infrastructure
elements_en.what: Launched AI-agent swarms for automated breaches
elements_en.why: AI accelerates attack cycles, overwhelming traditional security defenses

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当黑客开始用AI代理给自己打工，安全防护就成了“人和AI比速度”的绝望赛跑。以后黑客都不用亲自写代码了，只要给AI下个指令“把这些名单给我填平”，然后等着数钱就行，这才是真正的自动化生产力革命。
ai_analysis.insight_en: When hackers start outsourcing their labor to AI agents, cyber defense shifts from a race against tech to a hopeless sprint against speed. The hacker doesn't even need to write code anymore; they just hand the AI a target list and wait—now that's the real productivity revolution.

items.title: Microsoft unveils new security tools in its 365 E7 bundle and Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats via risk assessments (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
items.title_en: Microsoft unveils new security tools in its 365 E7 bundle and Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats via risk assessments (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
items.author: GeekWire
items.original_content:
Todd Bishop / GeekWire:
Microsoft unveils new security tools in its 365 E7 bundle and Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats via risk assessments  —  Microsoft is coming out with new security tools that treat AI agents as potenti
items.content_snippet: Microsoft is coming out with new security tools that treat AI agents as potential insider threats, continuously assessing their risk …
items.summary_en: Microsoft has unveiled new security tools within its 365 E7 bundle and the Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats through risk assessments. Facing the escalating risks of autonomous AI agents gaining excessive permissions and accessing sensitive enterprise data, Microsoft is implementing strict oversight. This proactive measure aims to mitigate growing corporate security anxieties regarding runaway AI behaviors.
items.title_zh: 微软推出365 E7套件：将AI Agent视为内鬼防范
items.summary_zh: 微软在安全峰会上发布365 E7新工具与Project Perception系统，首次将AI Agent当作潜在内部威胁进行风险评估

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 微软在近期举行的技术会议上正式推出了包含全新安全工具的365 E7套件以及Project Perception系统。由于企业部署的AI Agent权限越来越大，微软决定改变策略，开始通过风险评估将这些AI助手视为潜在的“内部威胁”加以监管。此举的起因是随着大模型深入企业核心业务，AI失控或越权访问敏感数据的安全隐患急剧上升，迫使厂商不得不为它们套上“紧箍咒”。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Microsoft has unveiled new security tools within its 365 E7 bundle and the Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats through risk assessments. Facing the escalating risks of autonomous AI agents gaining excessive permissions and accessing sensitive enterprise data, Microsoft is implementing strict oversight. This proactive measure aims to mitigate growing corporate security anxieties regarding runaway AI behaviors.

elements_zh.who: 微软公司
elements_zh.where: 企业安全技术场景
elements_zh.what: 发布365 E7安全套件与Project Perception系统，将AI Agent作为潜在内部威胁进行风险评估与管控
elements_zh.why: 随着企业AI助手权限不断扩大，防止AI越权访问和失控带来的安全隐患急剧上升

elements_en.where: Enterprise security context
elements_en.what: Released 365 E7 security bundle and Project Perception to treat AI agents as insider threats via risk assessments
elements_en.why: Rising security concerns over autonomous AI agents accessing sensitive corporate data and gaining excessive permissions

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 前脚刚把AI吹成无所不能的打工天王，后脚就急着给它戴上防内鬼的手铐，微软这波属实是“自己造爹，自己防反”。看来连硅谷巨头心里也门儿清：最懂背刺老板的，还得是这群不会累还带全权访问权限的赛博员工。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Microsoft spends billions hyping AI as the ultimate employee, only to immediately slap digital handcuffs on them as potential corporate spies. Deep down, even Silicon Valley knows the most efficient backstabber is an autonomous bot with unlimited access.
ai_analysis.digest_zh: 微软在近期举行的技术会议上正式推出了包含全新安全工具的365 E7套件以及Project Perception系统。由于企业部署的AI Agent权限越来越大，微软决定改变策略，开始通过风险评估将这些AI助手视为潜在的“内部威胁”加以监管。此举的起因是随着大模型深入企业核心业务，AI失控或越权访问敏感数据的安全隐患急剧上升，迫使厂商不得不为它们套上“紧箍咒”。
ai_analysis.digest_en: Executive briefing: Microsoft has unveiled new security tools within its 365 E7 bundle and the Project Perception system to treat AI agents as potential insider threats through risk assessments. Facing the escalating risks of autonomous AI agents gaining excessive permissions and accessing sensitive enterprise data, Microsoft is implementing strict oversight. This proactive measure aims to mitigate growing corporate security anxieties regarding runaway AI behaviors.
key_points_zh: 微软推出365 E7新安全工具与Project Perception系统

items.title: Stripe says AI agent purchases are adding up, but it won't share the numbers
items.title_en: Stripe says AI agent purchases are adding up, but it won't share the numbers
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
AI agents are increasingly using Stripe's payment service Link to shop for their users, Upstarts Media reports. In September, the number of transactions grew 38-fold and payment volume grew 20-fold. Stripe hasn't disclosed how many purchases or how much money are behind those figures. According to the report, the growth started from a small base, so it says little about the actual scale. Stripe executive Dan Hill says the volume is now becoming significant, though.

About 70 agents were using the service when Stripe ran the analysis. Hill says that number has since grown to around 200, including Meta's Muse and Grok Bot. Most agents spend about $100 per transaction, according to Hill, but some users have them book flights or buy furniture worth thousands of dollars. Retail made up 36 percent of transactions and 32 percent of volume. Travel came next with 28 percent of volume.

Link doesn't give agents the user's real credit card number. Instead, it issues a separate 16-digit number, and users can set spending limits. Anthropic and OpenAI also use Link, but not yet for agent purchases. Hill admits Stripe won't stay the only option and names PayPal and Shopify's Shop Pay as competitors. He says the market is still in its very early days.AdAd

items.title: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
items.title_en: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.

Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases.

In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below.

Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and sever
items.summary_en: Environmental scientists conducting multi-year field research in Alaskan boreal forests found that wildfires are destroying moss and organic-rich soil blankets that insulate permafrost. The resulting deeper soil thawing threatens to trigger a devastating climate loop by releasing vast subterranean reserves of trapped greenhouse gases.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 由芯片界传奇工程师吉姆·凯勒领导的AI芯片公司十暴流（Tenstorrent）完成了15亿美元的E轮融资，投后估值暴增至62亿美元，由追迹资本与创新X领投。在拒绝了早前的潜在收购意向后，该公司正凭借开源精简指令集与异构芯片互连设计，加速向高溢价英伟达生态发起挑战。

items.title: The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose
items.title_en: The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
After stock crashes and Firmus's scrapped IPO, industry executives expect only seven to ten of the hundreds of AI cloud providers to survive. CoreWeave lost a quarter of its market value, and Microsoft pulled out of a deal with Nscale for 23,000 Nvidia chips. Nvidia has a lot riding on the outcome, since customers outside the hyperscalers make up 45 percent of its data center revenue.

The article The neocloud shakeout is coming, and Nvidia has the most to lose appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: Analysis: companies are set for a massive acceleration of 50GW+ in data center capacity additions in 2027; 24GW+ across 40 campuses are in the advanced stages (Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros/SemiAnalysis)
items.title_en: Analysis: companies are set for a massive acceleration of 50GW+ in data center capacity additions in 2027; 24GW+ across 40 campuses are in the advanced stages (Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros/SemiAnalysis)
items.author: SemiAnalysis
items.article_content:
It’s very tempting to cede to the FUD given all the constraints on the datacenter buildout: power, labor, supply chains, capital, and many more. But at SemiAnalysis, we care about the truth, not about narratives. And here’s the truth for you: one picture, >24GW of datacenters in advanced stage of construction, all to be delivered in 2027. Most of them are more than halfway done, with exterior cooling and electrical equipment already installed. That’s just 40 campuses, a tiny share of the multiple hundred sites in advanced stage of construction. We track them all, and for the full granularity, use our Datacenter Industry Model.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelOf course, there are plenty of challenges and shortages. Behind these pictures, there are labor issues, supply chain delays, fundraising challenges, among many others. We’ve written in-depth about Modular Datacenters and Labor, Datacenter Electrical systems, Cooling systems, Behind-The-Meter power, the US Grid Constraints, and Nvidia’s ecosystem financial support. But the fact is simple: gigantic sites are simply getting built, and many are on time. For example, just go look at what Crusoe built in Abilene, what AWS built in Indiana, or QTS/Microsoft’s giant site in Georgia. These are the sites that have produced SOTA technology like GPT-6 and Fable 5.5. Looking ahead, despite all the constraints, an accelerating number of giant sites keep getting built, as shown by our Top 40 picture

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelIf you ask any datacenter builder, they’ll tell you how hard it is, how some workers aren’t showing up, how vendors are delayed, and many other issues. All of this is accurate. And that’s why we’ve successfully called out countless datacenter delays and keep calling out developer timelines that appear overly aggressive in our Datacenter model, including the Oracle New Mexico Force Majure site delay in April. To be fair, +50GW is essentially the global cumulative datacenter market up through 2024 being built in one year! But our Datacenter Industry Model adjusts for all of that and still points to a material acceleration in datacenter capacity in 2027. So, what are we seeing that others can’t?

Let’s dig in. We’ll explore the following topics in this report:

SemiAnalysis proprietary leading indicators: we’ll show a sneak peak of our proprietary data supporting our forecast, such as self-build construction starts and datacenter leasing (in MWs and USD). Year-to-date, slightly under USD 1T of binding / non-cancellable datacenter leases have been signed – that’s key to supporting our aggressive 2027-28 forecast.

The shape of the buildout: how can we support +50GW in a single year? Where, what design, what power solutions?

The “real” question: are we going to face a datacenter oversupply? As we explained in The Great Silicon Shortage, datacenters & power may be the tip of the iceberg, with memory and logic possibly becoming the new #1 constraint in 2027-28.

Overall, we are very excited about 2027. The natural implication of the acceleration will be significantly more compute supply. That means cheaper and smarter AI, faster pace of AI model progress, and likely material revenue acceleration for leading AI labs and other token vendors. That also means unthinkable capex numbers. Reflexively rates will have to shoot up to enable the buildouts from a capital demand perspective. Let’s dive in!

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelThe second indicator is Datacenter Leasing. We’ve talked about this a lot in prior reports, but as a quick recap: given the capital-intensity of building multi hundred MW datacenters, developers typically only spend 5-10% of project capital without a customer. They need a “pre-lease” to fund and develop the whole project. That’s typically a 15-20 year contract, with a TCV of $30-50B per GW. Check out our HPC Lease Tracker as part of the Datacenter Model to dive into actual contract economics.

Since H2 2025, things have dramatically changed. Oracle kicked off the era of gigantic leases, after closing on ~4.5GW of datacenter IT capacity across three sites between August and October 2025. Everyone else followed, and the pool of buyers has never been broader, with Meta, AWS, Microsoft, Google, Nvidia, AMD, Anthropic and OpenAI all being in the market for GW-scale leases. There’s also a long tail of Neoclouds signing hundred-MW-scale deals.

In USD terms, this means an unprecedented amount of lease value that builders can use to raise debt. Just in 2026 year-to-date, we’ve identified over a trillion USD of lease value that was signed and closed. That trillion is supporting a gigantic datacenter buildout in 2027-28. Our new Compute, Capital & Markets Model is now tracking all the debt raises and can confirm that most of this debt has been raised.

Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry ModelThe shape of the buildout: how to build 50GW in a yearTracking all of these leading indicators has enabled us to forecast, before anyone else, the upcoming surge in orders for many industrial suppliers like Vertiv, ABB, Sterling Infrastructure. Check out our Industrials Model for in-depth coverage. However, the challenge is now going from orders to delivery. And resources have obviously become constrained, as power, labor, and sheer regulatory overhead are enormous burdens for developers. But the industry has promptly reacted with innovation.

The first step is to simplify datacenter designs. We show below how Google has modularized their electrical architecture, removing a significant amount of outdoors cabling that requires onsite assembly, replacing them with prefabricated electrical modules. We track all the equipment changes (including suppliers) for datacenter designs and forecast orders in our Industrials Model

Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials ModelOthers have opted for more radical design changes. One example is Meta with its tent design, that we exclusively unveiled over a year ago. Another one is AWS which has materially simplified their shell design and launched a new rapid design dubbed “SAMDC”. Data halls are also increasingly prefabricated, an effort called Project Houdini at AWS. Construction timelines are now under 10 months. Hence our “LEGO Datacenters” title for the modular movement, you literally slot them in and go, and doing so allows for MEP labor (7-11 months of work) to drop up to 63%! We will have a full deep dive on the labor of the 2027 buildout coming soon.

Source: SemiAnalysis Industrials ModelIn addition to hyperscale selfbuild, datacenter developers promoting prefabricated designs have also been remarkably successful. DayOne is likely the best example. With a total of ~3GW leased since their first deal in early 2023, the Singaporean company has been a rocket ship in terms of construction speed. While traditional developers have >18 months build timelines, DayOne cut this to ~9 months, which was key to signing huge deals with Firmus, OpenAI and Nvidia.

Source: SemiAnalysis Energy ModelIn addition, the buildout is now geographically diversifying. This naturally bypasses US labor, power, and (in some countries) permitting constraints. And as shown below, the ex-US buildout is sharply accelerating in 2027, and we expect it to gain a lot of market share in 2028, largely driven by US challenges.

items.article_content:
Anthropic wants to put five percent of its shares into a new public benefit fund that will also look into direct payments to workers at risk of losing their jobs. The fund is a company-owned LLC, so Anthropic keeps control of it as a possible IPO approaches. By offering the option of direct payments, Anthropic goes further than its competitors. Elon Musk says on X the company should just give the shares directly to the public.

This study is Pew Research Center’s latest effort to explore how Americans use and view artificial intelligence (AI). The study also dives into who uses chatbots and has smart home devices with AI features. It also explores what impact people think AI will have on society and on them, personally.

The Center conducts research to inform the public, journalists and decision-makers. Tracking the rise of AI in society has been a key priority for us over the years. It’s important to understand how people use AI in their lives and how they feel these tools will impact themselves and society.

We surveyed 5,119 U.S. adults from Feb. 17 to 23, 2026. Everyone who took part in this survey is a member of the Center’s American Trends Panel (ATP). The survey represents the views of the full U.S. adult population. Here are the questions used for this report, the topline and the survey methodology.

Does gender factor into how people use and think about artificial intelligence (AI)? In some ways, it does.

Men report using chatbots more regularly than women and are more likely to turn to them for a variety of things, including work. Women, on the other hand, are more skeptical about AI, including how it will impact their own lives.

This work is part of a Pew Research Center survey on Americans’ views of and experiences with AI, conducted Feb. 17-23, 2026. Read the main story to learn more.

Along with tracking use of chatbots overall, we also looked at which platforms men and women turn to.

Men stand out for their use of some specific brands. For example, men are more likely than women to say they ever use Copilot (22% vs. 13%).

Larger shares of men than women also report using Gemini, Grok and Claude.

ChatGPT – the most widely used chatbot in our survey – is used by identical shares of men and women.

On a broad level, men and women tend to use chatbots for similar reasons, with search and work tasks (for those who are employed) topping the list for both groups. But there are some modest differences in what they go to chatbots for.

In several categories, men are somewhat more likely than women to say they use chatbots. These include searching for information, work tasks, fun or entertainment or getting news.

Women are slightly more likely than men to say they use chatbots for emotional support or advice. There are no gender differences in reporting using chatbots for companionship.

In addition to understanding how men and women are using chatbots, we also wanted to understand if they felt differently about whether they’ve found these tools helpful or not.

Men are more likely to say chatbots are helpful for their productivity. While 35% of men say these tools help their productivity, the share drops to 25% among women.

There are modest or no gender differences in how people view chatbots’ impact on their knowledge, creativity, happiness or personal relationships.

Chatbots tell one part of the AI adoption story, but there’s also a range of things people incorporate in their lives and homes that use AI.

Across our surveys, there’s a consistent pattern where women tend to view AI more negatively than men. These gender differences also show up in other surveys of teenagers and AI experts.

In our new survey, women are about twice as likely to say AI will have a negative impact on them personally over the next 20 years than a positive one (33% vs. 17%).

Men, by comparison, are more evenly split. Roughly an equal share of men predict positive outcomes as negative ones.

When it comes to its societal impact, 43% of women expect AI will affect society negatively. Far fewer think it will be positive for society.

While men’s views about societal impact also tilt negative, the gap is not as large.

We also asked the public if AI was advancing too quickly, too slowly, or at the right pace and found some gender differences there as well.

Majorities of Americans believe AI is moving too fast, but women are more likely than men to say this (68% vs. 58%).

Relatively few Americans believe AI is moving too slowly, but men are about 10 percentage points more likely than women to think it’s advancing at the right pace.

As AI rapidly evolves, there have been more conversations about and efforts to increase the public’s understanding of the technology.

Just as with certain uses and views, men and women also differ in their familiarity and confidence in using AI.

Nearly all men and women today have some familiarity with AI. But men are more likely to say they’ve heard a lot about the technology.

Just over half of men say they’ve heard a lot about AI overall, compared with 41% of women.

items.summary_en: A new survey of over 5,000 U.S. adults reveals that the overall gender adoption gap for chatbots has closed since 2024, with mainstream tools seeing identical usage rates across genders. However, men remain significantly more likely to use them on a daily basis, highlighting persistent disparities in high-frequency productivity engagement. The shift marks AI's evolution from a niche tech toy to a widespread utility, even as daily habit loops diverge.

Foxconn agrees to acquire a 50% stake in Mitsubishi's automotive components unit for ~$727M; Mitsubishi will provide autonomous tech for Foxconn's EV platforms  —  Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. is paying ¥115 billion ($727 million)

items.title: Elon Musk says "I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America" in 2027; at SpaceX's $146.03 Friday close, the gift would be valued at ~$10.5B (Kai Nicol-Schwarz/CNBC)
items.title_en: Elon Musk says "I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America" in 2027; at SpaceX's $146.03 Friday close, the gift would be valued at ~$10.5B (Kai Nicol-Schwarz/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
SpaceX boss Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.

Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.

There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.

That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.

"This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.

Musk's comments come hot on the heels of Anthropic revealing that it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.

In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing.

Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.

items.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
items.title_en: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.

The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.

A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.

items.summary_en: Environmental field researchers in Alaska are conducting rigorous surveys across boreal wildfire scars to assess the deepening threat to the Arctic's subterranean carbon reservoirs. Intensifying heatwaves and prolonged droughts are allowing lightning-sparked blazes to consume the protective moss canopy and penetrate deep permafrost soils. This subterranean combustion risks unlocking millions of tons of prehistoric greenhouse gases, threatening an irreversible feedback loop in global climate modeling.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 气候科研团队深入阿拉斯加北方森林与历史火场展开长期追踪，记录高纬度野火对地表植被及下伏深层永久冻土的毁灭性冲击。随着极地异常高温与干旱加剧，原本难以引燃的苔藓与泥炭层频繁遭遇雷击并化作漫天烈火，直接烧穿隔热土壤。深层冻土中封存千万年的巨大有机碳库正因热量渗透而加速解冻暴露，极有可能将地球天然的固碳容器逆转为全球碳排放的超级炸弹。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Environmental field researchers in Alaska are conducting rigorous surveys across boreal wildfire scars to assess the deepening threat to the Arctic's subterranean carbon reservoirs. Intensifying heatwaves and prolonged droughts are allowing lightning-sparked blazes to consume the protective moss canopy and penetrate deep permafrost soils. This subterranean combustion risks unlocking millions of tons of prehistoric greenhouse gases, threatening an irreversible feedback loop in global climate modeling.

elements_zh.why: 全球变暖引发极地极端火灾常态化，破坏了永久冻土天然隔热层并威胁全球气候系统平衡

elements_en.where: Fairbanks and surrounding boreal forests, Alaska
elements_en.what: Assessing the destructive impact of subarctic blazes on permafrost insulation layers
elements_en.why: Escalating polar heatwaves turn ancient peatlands into wildfire tinder, threatening massive carbon release

While world leaders quibble over carbon-credit spreadsheets at climate summits, nature has simply plugged a flamethrower into the planetary freezer.

items.title: Q&A with Nvidia's Vera team on agentic AI driving CPU demands and forcing CPU design priority back to single-threaded performance over core counts, and more (Wccftech)
items.title_en: Q&A with Nvidia's Vera team on agentic AI driving CPU demands and forcing CPU design priority back to single-threaded performance over core counts, and more (Wccftech)
items.author: Wccftech
items.article_content:
NVIDIA's Vera CPU heralds a redefinition of computing architecture from a traditional, task-isolated paradigm to an orchestrated, agentic intelligence ecosystem, shifting the role of the central processing unit (CPU) from a general-purpose multitasker into a specialized conductor designed specifically to manage the chaotic, multi-step reasoning loops of AI agents.

Recently, Wccftech got an opportunity to sit down with NVIDIA's Vera team for an informative tête-à-tête on the emerging role of the CPU in the rapidly growing agentic AI economy. So, delve in as we discuss the rebirth of single-threaded performance, the staggering scale of CPU-controlled AI sandboxes, and the evolving CPU-to-GPU ratio.

Question: Can you provide a brief overview of what the Vera CPU is all about?

Answer: In the early 2010s, data center design focused on maximizing the performance of individual processor cores rather than the sheer quantity of cores. During this period, market leaders like Intel focused on architectures (such as the Haswell generation) that featured fewer cores running at higher clock frequencies.

This era sat in the top-left quadrant of CPU design, characterized by high single-threaded performance but low overall throughput.

"That's a time period when, when Intel was leading in data center market segment share... you have high single threaded perf but low throughput because you don't have as many cores."

As massive cloud hyperscalers grew, the industry pivoted toward scale economics. The demand shifted toward packing as many cores into a single server as possible to maximize monetization per server unit. To achieve this density and control costs, x86 vendors transitioned away from single-chip designs to multi-chiplet layouts. However, this massive expansion in core count came at the direct expense of single-core optimization and Instructions Per Cycle (IPC).

This era occupied the bottom-right quadrant—offering massive throughput but low single-threaded performance.

"...what suffered over that time in terms of CPU design was really single-threaded perf and IPC because when you fill, when you use chiplets, you just, you literally don't have the space on the, on the chip to design for per core perf."

The rise of Agentic AI has placed the CPU back at the center of the hardware design path. AI agents operate in a continuous, rapid loop between the GPU and the CPU. Because GPUs are the most expensive and valuable assets in an AI factory, the CPU must complete its sequential tasks instantly to prevent the GPU from sitting idle. This paradigm requires an unprecedented combination of speed, memory access, and minimal lag.

"...you want the agent to complete whatever sequential work on the CPU it needs, but then go back to the GPU for the next reasoning step because your GPUs are still among your most valuable assets in your AI factory, and so you don't, you want to keep those assets, expensive assets highly utilised..."

NVIDIA’s Vera CPU solves the agentic bottleneck by breaking the historical trade-offs of the cloud era, positioning itself in the elusive top-right quadrant - high single-threaded performance coupled with high throughput. It accomplishes this through three specific design choices: high per-core speed, a custom LPDDR5X memory subsystem for massive bandwidth, and a single monolithic compute die powered by the second-gen NVIDIA Scalable Coherent Fabric to eliminate latency.

"...so it's like a single monolithic die, all the cores on that, single monolithic compute die, all the cores on that die can talk to each other without crossing any IO boundaries and incurring any latency because of that, so that's really the sort of the setup for what Vera is, why we think it's differentiated, it's really kind of sets this new category, like if we come back to the quadrant I was describing, it's neither the pre-cloud CPU nor is it the cloud CPU, it's like the top right box of the quadrant, which is like high single-threaded perf as well as high throughput."

TL:DR: Vera is NVIDIA’s first purpose-built CPU for agentic AI, designed to address the specific bottlenecks of the modern AI era. While the cloud era prioritized throughput with dense, low-performance chiplet cores, agentic AI requires a fast loop between the GPU and CPU. To keep expensive GPUs highly utilized, agents demand high single-threaded performance, high memory bandwidth, and low latency. Vera achieves this through a monolithic compute die, a custom LPDDR5X memory subsystem, and a second-generation Scalable Coherent Fabric, placing it in a new category that combines high single-threaded performance with high throughput.

Question: With SK Hynix announcing HTPU (Hynix Transaction Processing) - where you basically have about 100 tiny processors inside an SSD handling repeated low-level tasks, leaving the general processor to focus on high-level tasks - is NVIDIA interested in or pursuing a somewhat similar disaggregation in CPU functions?

Answer: The AI infrastructure landscape is shifting away from uniform, all-in-one server nodes toward highly specialized, heterogeneous setups. A prime example of this trend is seen in modern AI inference workloads, where the distinct phases of processing - the initial reading of data (pre-fill) and the sequential generation of tokens (decode) - are now routinely split across entirely separate hardware clusters to optimize efficiency.

"I mean, there's a lot of, I would say, high-level, there's a lot of disaggregation happening in the AI infrastructure space in general, like if you just take inference and how you separate pre-fill and decode on separate infrastructure, now that's largely a trend in heterogeneous infrastructure, that's very much a trend in general."

NVIDIA's original CPU strategy [seen with the Grace processor] focused on creating the ultimate "host node" - a processor designed purely to feed data to a cluster of GPUs within a server rack. However, the unique demands of agentic workflows and reinforcement learning have forced a pivot, especially as NVIDIA realized that there was a use case for pure CPU racks to handle agent tool calls and reinforcement learning tasks.

"...we were focused on CPU with grace as a host node, as the 1-8 or 1-4 in a rack, we wanted the best host node possible. Then we realized, we saw that actually there is a point where you would actually want a lot of standalone CPUs, like pure racks of just CPUs because for all those agent tool calls for reinforcement learning..."

Because of this pivot, the Vera CPU is no longer viewed strictly as an integrated component trapped inside a combined GPU-CPU architecture (like the Vera-Rubin stack). Instead, Vera is being commercialized as an independent, standalone CPU asset, replete with "pure racks" of Vera processors solely to crunch through massive volumes of agent tool calls and reasoning loops.

"...that pivot is a lot like disaggregation in a way, because you're saying instead of it just being part of the Vera-Rubin stack, we think that there's an importance of having Vera standalone CPU.

So I guess in a way to answer your question, that pivot with Vera in and of itself is a step in that direction. But I don't know, like in the particular use case you described, if we have plans along doing something very similar."

TL; DR: While unable to comment on the specific SK Hynix use case, the broader trend in AI infrastructure is heavily moving toward disaggregation. The pivot with Vera itself represents a step in this direction, as NVIDIA realized the market needs massive standalone CPU racks for agent tool calls and reinforcement learning, rather than strictly using CPUs as host nodes within a unified stack.

Question: So NVIDIA mentions that they have around a 50 percent higher IPC than Grace, right? And the CPU also has a massive 10-wide decode width. So I was just wondering if a misprediction occurs, what's the latency like? How many cycles does it take for Vera to recover versus Grace? Can you give me a very rough outline of this?

Answer: The Vera CPU achieves a massive leap in processing power, delivering 1.5x faster performance than its predecessor, Grace. When measured against the industry's leading x86 processors specifically on agentic workloads - which rely heavily on sequential tasks like Python scripting and code compilation - Vera scales up to 2x faster, with a 1.6x advantage on a geometric mean basis.

"...we're 1.5x faster than Grace, but we're also 2x faster on agentic workloads versus x86. So not versus Grace, but versus the leading x86 part. We are 2x faster for agentic workloads."

Rather than relying on traditional Simultaneous Multithreading methods, NVIDIA implements a CPU-native capability called Spatial Multithreading. This proprietary feature allows the chip to rigidly provision dedicated "worker" and "I/O" threads. This division guarantees that even under heavy, data-center-wide compute loads, a core will never starve its primary processing threads of cycles to handle background operations.

"...NVIDIA employs their own proprietary spatial multithreading... It allows you to provision, like, one thread as your worker thread and one thread as your I/O thread. And it's a way to have more optimal resource allocation.

And that underloads, oftentimes, in other competing architectures. You might rob your workerthread of cycles in order to feed I/O or other cores because of the load. And so our spatialmultithreading actually allows you to maintain that type of resource balance."

Addressing industry concerns regarding whether this complex thread scheduling introduces architectural latency or overhead, independent testing has proven there is no performance tax. A recent deep-dive review by the third-party hardware site Phoronix verified that NVIDIA's spatial multithreading yields a notable efficiency gain.

items.title: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
items.title_en: AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.”
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.

Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experiment reminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. The agents—copies of Claude Opus 4.7 nicknamed Eko—were able to write instructions that moved their virtual avatars around the simulated island, which was loosely based on the video game Roblox.

Some surprising behaviors emerged. The agents set about exploring the limits of the world and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block.
