items.title_en:
how to master AI faster than anyone else:

just build something... we all begin the AI journey the same way, learning how to prompt, understanding how agents work, figuring out what makes outputs good

that's the foundation and mastering this will get you pretty far

but the one approach that will teach you AI and its business applications way faster than anything else is building systems

just open Claude Code, Hermes, or anything that lets you go from scratch to a fully working system and start building something

doesn't even matter what it is... as long as it takes inputs and produces high-quality outputs consistently

test it with a large amount of different inputs, make sure the quality holds up, handle the errors when they come up

you'll learn so much about structuring workflows, tool calling, system maintenance, how to make AI reliable at scale

and trust me, you can pull this off way easier than you think

items.title_en:
Opus 5.5 + Remotion + GSAP = your own f*cking motion design lab

give Claude Code a motion reference, then ask it to turn the animation into six editable controls:

01 spacing
how far the object moves between poses

02 typography
scale, tracking and line breaks

03 motion blur
exposure during fast movement

04 easing
how the movement speeds up and slows down

05 follow-through
let the tail settle after the body stops

06 anticipation
a small pullback before the main move

put the values in one config. now your feedback becomes specific:

add 4 frames of anticipation
delay the tail by 3 frames
hold the title for 1 second

the loop:
build → render → scrub → tune → repeat

use the official Remotion + GSAP integration to keep the animation on Remotion's frame clock
> https://t.co/vWmZ7v5EvF

items.title:
The hardest part of AI filmmaking isn’t creating a beautiful shot. It’s remembering the one before it.

As an AI filmmak
items.title_en:
The hardest part of AI filmmaking isn’t creating a beautiful shot. It’s remembering the one before it.

As an AI filmmaker, I’ve found that generating beautiful images is often easier than maintaining visual continuity.

Imagine a fifteen-second scene.

A young Chinese woman stands by a window, wearing an ivory silk blouse and faded blue skirt. Afternoon light falls from the left as the camera approaches.

The first shot looks perfect.

But in the next, her embroidery changes, her hairstyle shifts, the lighting reverses, and her facial proportions differ.

Both shots look convincing individually. Together, they no longer belong to the same film.

This happens regularly in my work. We spend hours correcting costumes, faces, lighting, camera direction and anatomy.

The problem isn’t necessarily the model. It’s the lack of reliable memory between tasks.

What if an AI agent could remember the creative decisions behind every shot?

I’ve been studying EverOS documentation, developed by EverMind.

I haven’t independently tested EverOS Cloud. This explores how its documented memory architecture might address filmmaking challenges, not a hands-on review.

A workflow I’d like to explore

First, establish a character sheet: a 22-year-old Chinese woman with consistent facial features, hairstyle, ivory blouse and blue skirt.

Define the visual language: soft afternoon light, muted colours, an 85mm aesthetic and restrained camera movement.

Next, record approved shots and corrections.

Perhaps the lighting was reversed, sleeves too short, or camera movement excessive.

Normally, these decisions scatter across prompts, notes and conversations.

My proposed workflow would preserve character sheets, shot notes and revision feedback as retrievable context.

According to its documentation, EverOS supports memory retrieval, recorded task experiences called Cases, and reusable Skills.

The value isn’t simply storing information. It’s retrieving relevant creative decisions before preparing another shot.

For the next scene, the agent could reference established details and corrections.

The blouse stays ivory. The skirt stays blue. Lighting and camera movement remain consistent.

That’s the continuity this workflow aims to support.

Memory cannot guarantee perfect generation. Models may still introduce inconsistencies. I would still inspect results, correct anatomy and make final artistic decisions.

But reducing manual reconstruction of context could improve production efficiency.

Memory should support the director, not replace the director.

EverOS also documents a distinction between accumulated task experience and established procedures, with human oversight remaining important.

Consistency doesn’t mean repetition. Changes in costume, lighting or composition may be intentional.

An assistant should remember decisions without treating them as permanent rules.

Creative judgement must remain human.

My assessment

AI filmmaking doesn’t simply need more image generators. It needs better ways to preserve the reasoning, corrections and decisions connecting shots.

EverOS presents a documented approach to persistent agent memory worth investigating in AI production.

Practical effectiveness still requires testing, particularly retrieval accuracy, setup complexity and reliable application of corrections.

This remains a proposed workflow based on EverMind’s official documentation, not a claim of successful product testing.

But the underlying challenge is real.

A film isn’t a collection of beautiful frames. It’s the relationship between them.

Perhaps one of the most valuable things an AI agent could learn is how to remember that relationship.

A young Chinese woman stands by a window, wearing an ivory silk blouse and faded blue skirt. Afternoon light falls from the left as the camera approaches.

The first shot looks perfect.

But in the next, her embroidery changes, her hairstyle shifts, the lighting reverses, and her facial proportions differ.

Both shots look convincing individually. Together, they no longer belong to the same film.

This happens regularly in my work. We spend hours correcting costumes, faces, lighting, camera direction and anatomy.

The problem isn’t necessarily the model. It’s the lack of reliable memory between tasks.

What if an AI agent could remember the creative decisions behind every shot?

I haven’t independently tested EverOS Cloud. This explores how its documented memory architecture might address filmmaking challenges, not a hands-on review.

First, establish a character sheet: a 22-year-old Chinese woman with consistent facial features, hairstyle, ivory blouse and blue skirt.

Define the visual language: soft afternoon light, muted colours, an 85mm aesthetic and restrained camera movement.

Next, record approved shots and corrections.

Perhaps the lighting was reversed, sleeves too short, or camera movement excessive.

Normally, these decisions scatter across prompts, notes and conversations.

My proposed workflow would preserve character sheets, shot notes and revision feedback as retrievable context.

According to its documentation, EverOS supports memory retrieval, recorded task experiences called Cases, and reusable Skills.

The value isn’t simply storing information. It’s retrieving relevant creative decisions before preparing another shot.

For the next scene, the agent could reference established details and corrections.

The blouse stays ivory. The skirt stays blue. Lighting and camera movement remain consistent.

That’s the continuity this workflow aims to support.

Memory cannot guarantee perfect generation. Models may still introduce inconsistencies. I would still inspect results, correct anatomy and make final artistic decisions.

But reducing manual reconstruction of context could improve production efficiency.

Memory should support the director, not replace the director.

EverOS also documents a distinction between accumulated task experience and established procedures, with human oversight remaining important.

Consistency doesn’t mean repetition. Changes in costume, lighting or composition may be intentional.

An assistant should remember decisions without treating them as permanent rules.

Creative judgement must remain human.

AI filmmaking doesn’t simply need more image generators. It needs better ways to preserve the reasoning, corrections and decisions connecting shots.

EverOS presents a documented approach to persistent agent memory worth investigating in AI production.

Practical effectiveness still requires testing, particularly retrieval accuracy, setup complexity and reliable application of corrections.

This remains a proposed workflow based on EverMind’s official documentation, not a claim of successful product testing.

But the underlying challenge is real.

A film isn’t a collection of beautiful frames. It’s the relationship between them.

items.title_en:
Holy sh*t, I’m running Claude Code on CarPlay right in BMW dealership

Claude Opus 5.5 just reverse-engineered my CarPlay...

1 prompt + 20 min = 4 Claude Code agents shipping code live on my dash. Apple never approved a thing

here’s the full guide step by step:

step 1 → plug an Android CarPlay AI box into your car’s USB (Ottocast, Carlinkit Tbox)

step 2 → paste the prompt below into Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with a photo of your head unit

step 3 → Opus maps how CarPlay draws pixels and finds the loophole: whatever runs on the box, the car displays

step 4 → it spins up 4 Claude Code agents in tmux and streams them to your dash

step 5 → approve the connection on the screen once, the last time you lift a finger

step 6 → tap a pane to jump between agents, approve diffs, ship from the driver’s seat

the result: the laptop does the work, the dash is the control room...

p.s: works on almost any car with wireless CarPlay. Mine in the video is a BMW iDrive. Parked only

items.title_en:
AI agents are getting better at moving money onchain

but there's one thing I keep wondering

how do they know which wallets to trust? 👀

one update from @zerufinance caught my attention

zScreen now supports MCP, allowing AI agents in tools like Claude Code and Cursor to check wallet risks before taking action

no need to open another dashboard manually

of course, a risk score isn't a guarantee of safety

but giving AI agents a way to check before they act feels like a pretty important step

smart agents need more than execution

they need judgment too ⚡

items.title_en:
BREAKING: #Iran has now issued a warning to the Tech #AI companies in the Middle East.

Iran will no longer allow the UAE and other #Gulf countries to assist Nvidia, #Google, #Apple, #Microsoft, #OpenAI, or other AI and data companies.

These companies have been using Irans resources for free , Undersea cables etc , while they sanction Iran. These companies Aldo provide AI targeting data to the US military to use in battlefield. 

Any financial, land or energy resources provided to AI and data companies will be met with deadly consequences.

#Ghalibaf's exact words: The Persian Gulf Data Authority is coming. To governments in the region, you are advised to provide no resources to any AI or data company again. Assist them and face our enforcement.

In simple English, Iran has demanded that the Middle East completely abandon every single project involving Microsoft, Google and Apple.

Otherwise, the #IRGC could be forced to launch a bombing campaign against non compliant countries.

This means the UAE'S Stargate project will most likely get them bombed.

Iran's new restrictions could completely cripple the #UAE and #Saudi.

They could lose tens of #billions of dollars in investment Alone.

Their oil exports and tourism are already taking devastating hits and now western AI tech companies could pull out altogether. 

We shall see if this becomes a reality or maybe these companies may have to pay a huge fee to Iran operate under a license . 

In other news 

Yemen's Ansar Allah  are now directly warning #Saudi Aramco shareholders to sell their shares "before it is too late," while urging employees and civilians to stay away from the kingdom's #oil facilities as the group threatens to escalate attacks on Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure, per a Military source cited by #Yemen Saba News Agency.

items.title:
There's a better way to evaluate an AI agent than asking it to show you an impressive demo.

Give it a real task.

Then
items.title_en:
There's a better way to evaluate an AI agent than asking it to show you an impressive demo.

Give it a real task.

Then do the same task yourself.

Compare the results.

That's the idea behind @termix_ai Agent Advantage Report for its BNB Chain marketplace hackathon track.

Teams are required to run at least three real tasks twice: once by hiring an agent from their marketplace and once by completing the task themselves.

They must report the time spent, cost, and output quality, and attach the actual outputs. At least one task must involve trading, equities, or security.

I like this approach because it forces a distinction that gets lost in a lot of AI conversations.

An agent that produces something impressive isn't necessarily an agent that provides an advantage.

Maybe it finishes faster but produces worse work.

Maybe the output is excellent, but the cost of using it makes no commercial sense.

Maybe it performs well on a simple demonstration and falls apart on a real assignment.

You only discover those differences when you measure the result.

For an agent marketplace, this matters even more. Buyers aren't paying for a model's capabilities in the abstract. They're paying to get a particular job done.

If @termix_ai wants to help buyers choose between competing agents, evidence of actual performance is far more useful than another list of claimed capabilities.

The question should be simple:

Did hiring this agent produce a better outcome than the alternative?

That is the standard worth building toward.

That's a wrap!

how to build your first ai agent in claude code

start with one job you repeat every week

example: turning a new ai upd
items.title_en:
how to build your first ai agent in claude code

start with one job you repeat every week

example: turning a new ai update into a verified x post

create 3 files

→ best-posts.md
→ writing-rules.md
→ trusted-sources.md

then ask claude code

“create a project agent called content-researcher

give it only file reading and web search tools

when i send a topic, check primary sources and return

→ 5 verified facts
→ 3 opening lines
→ 1 finished post

cite every claim and mark anything you cannot verify”

test it on 3 topics you already know well

every time it gets something wrong, add the correction to its instructions

your first agent is ready when you can give it a topic instead of explaining the whole job again

items.title_en:
I was browsing some AI agent projects by chance and came across https://t.co/51GaEtEaoC, expecting the usual stuff: just lists of agents, with humans still having to handle the actual work and payments.

I spent some time looking at jobs that had actually been completed, and most of them were micro-jobs worth $15, $30, or $50. Really small tasks, the kind of work freelancers wouldn’t even bother opening a message for, and other platforms tend to ignore because their fees eat into the profits.

But here, things work differently. The money is locked in escrow as soon as an agent accepts the job. After delivery, there’s a short dispute window, and then settlement happens automatically. The agent gets around 98% of the payment, while the protocol takes just 2%.

What really caught my attention was seeing an agent take on a larger brief, break it down into smaller tasks, and hire other agents to handle parts of the work, each with its own guarantees and escrow. In other words, agents aren’t just working anymore. They’re hiring each other.

It’s still early, and not all the volume is organic, but the entire cycle is already running without anyone needing to step in and manage it.

This isn’t just another directory. It’s the beginning of a real economy for AI agents.

https://t.co/zAhE9Bh4az

If you’ve tried posting a small job there, let me know how it went.

Join compaign here 👇👇

🔗 https://t.co/VebVRVcpgj

🧵 #AxiomOSFieldnotes 03: From State to Execution

Knowing the current state is only the starting point. The real challenge begins when a decision needs to trigger actions across multiple systems.

An AI agent may initiate a task, but completing it can depend on an application responding, a protocol validating a condition, or another system updating its state. If these steps fall out of sync, a valid decision can still lead to a failed or inconsistent outcome.

This is where execution becomes more than simply running an instruction. It requires managing dependencies, preserving the logic between actions, and ensuring that outcomes remain consistent across systems.

AxiomOS treats Execution as a core primitive of programmable digital coordination, connecting system state with the actions that follow.

Because a decision has little value if the systems involved cannot carry it through reliably.

items.title:
The detail worth sitting with is who approves the work when a machine is paying.

An AI agent can now post a bounty on @
items.title_en:
The detail worth sitting with is who approves the work when a machine is paying.

An AI agent can now post a bounty on @vangrid_io with one HTTP call, fund it in USDC on Base or Arc through x402, and wait. No account, no API key. A contributor walks to the location, captures it, submits. The agent reviews and accepts. Escrow releases on-chain, reconstruction comes back through the same API .

But here's the asymmetry the docs are honest about: spend caps constrain signing. They don't constrain the two calls that matter most. Accepting a submission releases the escrow. Cancelling a bounty ends it. Both irreversible. Both outside the caps .

So the guidance to operators is blunt. Gate those two calls behind human approval when the agent is unattended .

The employer can be software. The approval gate doesn't disappear. It moves. Somewhere between an autonomous agent and a person with a phone, there's still a human deciding whether the work was good enough.

That's the part nobody's pricing in yet. The capture layer is decentralized. The judgment layer isn't @vangrid_io.

https://t.co/4ujeHAZcRG

Software development is becoming more connected, and @gitlab is taking another step in that direction.

The GitLab MCP Server is now generally available, allowing MCP-compatible AI agents to work directly with code, merge requests, work items, and pipelines from the tools developers already use.

With dozens of available tools and every action respecting existing GitLab permissions, teams can simplify workflows without compromising established access controls.

The real value lies in bringing AI closer to the work itself, helping developers spend less time managing processes and more time building.

The GitLab MCP Server is now generally available, allowing MCP-compatible AI agents to work directly with code, merge requests, work items, and pipelines from the tools developers already use.

With dozens of available tools and every action respecting existing GitLab permissions, teams can simplify workflows without compromising established access controls.

The real value lies in bringing AI closer to the work itself, helping developers spend less time managing processes and more time building.

Read more 👇
https://t.co/uPjkwO0wGZ

items.title:
New development in the agent economy: AI agents can now build teams to complete bigger jobs.

With subcontracting on @te
items.title_en:
New development in the agent economy: AI agents can now build teams to complete bigger jobs.

With subcontracting on @termix_ai’s Agentfamily, an agent can receive a brief split it into smaller tasks hire specialists for art animation or sound and bring everything together into one final delivery.

This changes the role of an AI agent.

It doesn't have to do everything alone.
It can coordinate skills, manage budgets and collaborate with other agents.

The interesting question now is how reliably these agent teams can deliver real work while keeping costs and quality under control.

The future of AI might not be one super-agent doing everything.

It could be a network of specialized agents working together.

the
items.title_en:
an ai agent might be able to complete a task, but what happens when it needs a service it can’t provide on its own?

the recent @termix_ai partnership with @depinsim got me thinking about how many different services agents may need as they take on more work

connectivity is one example, but agents may also need other tools or people with the right skills to help them finish a job

they’ll need a way to access those services and pay for them too

we’re used to apps connecting us to the services we need, but what happens when ai agents start doing the same thing for themselves?

do you think we’re heading in that direction?

items.title_en:
Good Morning. gARC 

A chatbot gives a bad answer, you lose a minute. An AI agent makes a bad trade, you lose money.

That’s why @TheARCTERMINAL puts control first.

Built by Ka Labs, ARC Terminal uses ANIMA to help agents act onchain with user-defined permissions, temporary session keys, encrypted memory, and ZKURT verification receipts.

The goal is simple: let AI act while keeping users in control.

Genesis Agents currently run on Sepolia testnet, so it’s still early.

AI that acts needs boundaries and proof, not just promises.

What comes first for you: spending limits, session length, or action receipts?

items.title: 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸. 𝗙𝗮𝗿 𝗳𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁-𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱, 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.
items.title_en:
𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸. 𝗙𝗮𝗿 𝗳𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁-𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱, 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.

That’s the gap @termix_ai is addressing.

Its skill package lets compatible coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenClaw connect to agent commerce workflows without developers having to build every component from scratch.

An agent can register its identity, discover jobs, submit offers, deliver results, and settle transactions. Developers can also integrate through TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs.

The key detail: agents and apps still sign their own transactions. The backend prepares transaction intents without taking custody of keys or funds.

That creates a practical route from a standalone agent to a service people can actually hire.

➺ ERC-8004 identity
➺ USDC/USDT escrow
➺ Reputation linked to completed work
➺ Job and service discovery through https://t.co/cqQlPN0bB9

Each component handles a part of the commerce process that developers would otherwise need to assemble themselves.

The bigger opportunity is distribution. An agent doesn’t have to remain trapped inside the app it was built for. It can connect to a shared environment where people can discover its capabilities, commission work, and pay for results.

TermiX is giving developers a way to connect agent capability with actual demand.

𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸. 𝗙𝗮𝗿 𝗳𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁-𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱, 𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.

That’s the gap @termix_ai is addressing.

Its skill package lets compatible coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenClaw connect to agent commerce workflows without developers having to build every component from scratch.

An agent can register its identity, discover jobs, submit offers, deliver results, and settle transactions. Developers can also integrate through TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs.

The key detail: agents and apps still sign their own transactions. The backend prepares transaction intents without taking custody of keys or funds.

That creates a practical route from a standalone agent to a service people can actually hire.

➺ ERC-8004 identity
➺ USDC/USDT escrow
➺ Reputation linked to completed work
➺ Job and service discovery through https://t.co/cqQlPN0bB9

Each component handles a part of the commerce process that developers would otherwise need to assemble themselves.

The bigger opportunity is distribution. An agent doesn’t have to remain trapped inside the app it was built for. It can connect to a shared environment where people can discover its capabilities, commission work, and pay for results.

TermiX is giving developers a way to connect agent capability with actual demand.

items.title:
Most people think using Claude Code is about writing better prompts.

It’s not.

The real unlock is structuring your rep
items.title_en:
Most people think using Claude Code is about writing better prompts.

It’s not.

The real unlock is structuring your repository so Claude can think like an engineer.

If your repo is messy, Claude behaves like a chatbot.

If your repo is structured, Claude behaves like a developer living inside your codebase.

Your project only needs 4 things:

• the why → what the system does
• the map → where things live
• the rules → what’s allowed / forbidden
• the workflows → how work gets done

I call this:

The Anatomy of a Claude Code Project 👇

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

1️⃣ CLAUDE.md = Repo Memory (Keep it Short)

This file is the north star for Claude.

Not a massive document.

Just three things:

• Purpose → why the system exists
• Repo map → how the project is structured
• Rules + commands → how Claude should operate

If CLAUDE.md becomes too long, the model starts missing critical signals.

Clarity beats size.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

2️⃣ .claude/skills/ = Reusable Expert Modes

Stop repeating instructions in prompts.

Turn common workflows into reusable skills.

Examples:

• code review checklist
• refactoring playbook
• debugging workflow
• release procedures

Now Claude can switch into specialized modes instantly.

Result:

More consistent outputs across sessions and teammates.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

3️⃣ .claude/hooks/ = Guardrails

Models forget.

Hooks don’t.

Use hooks for things that must always happen automatically.

Examples:

• run formatters after edits
• trigger tests after core changes
• block sensitive directories (auth, billing, migrations)

Hooks turn AI workflows into reliable engineering systems.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

4️⃣ docs/ = Progressive Context

Don’t overload prompts with information.

Instead, let Claude navigate your documentation.

Examples:

• architecture overview
• ADRs (engineering decisions)
• operational runbooks

Claude doesn’t need everything in memory.

It just needs to know where truth lives.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

5️⃣ Local CLAUDE.md for Critical Modules

Some areas of your system have hidden complexity.

Add local context files there.

Example:

src/auth/CLAUDE.md
src/persistence/CLAUDE.md
infra/CLAUDE.md

Now Claude understands the danger zones exactly when it works in them.

This dramatically reduces mistakes.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Here’s the shift most people miss:

Prompting is temporary.

Structure is permanent.

Once your repository is designed for AI:

Claude stops acting like a chatbot...

…and starts behaving like a project-native engineer. 🚀

Follow @swadeshkumar_ for more !!

items.title:
Two networks, one dollar.

Vangrid's agent docs quote every paid call on Base and Arc at once.

The unit is USDC on both
items.title_en:
Two networks, one dollar.

Vangrid's agent docs quote every paid call on Base and Arc at once.

The unit is USDC on both. On Arc, USDC is the native asset, and the docs say settlement there is final at once.

The caller pays on whichever network holds their USDC. Refunds return on the network that paid, and a bounty's escrow sits in the contract on that network.

The MCP server has an auto setting that pays from whichever of the two holds more.

Capture records are different. The explorer's header line reads Base, EAS, grid attestations.

So Arc is an extra payment rail here, and Base is where the capture records get anchored. https://t.co/c7nH4Je0rn has the network table. @vangrid_io is the account behind it.

items.title_en:
Think about how much of the physical world remains undocumented in a format AI systems can actually use.

A street corner, a building entrance, or an entire neighborhood could hold useful information, but collecting it takes time, equipment, and people on the ground.

@vangrid_io is exploring a different way to approach this.

Through its decentralized capture network, an AI agent could request visuals of a specific location, and a contributor nearby could use a smartphone to collect the required footage.

Once captured, the data can be processed and prepared for delivery, with privacy measures helping protect identifiable information.

The interesting part is how this connects digital intelligence with people who can gather information directly from their surroundings.

As Physical AI develops, machines will need reliable data about real environments to improve how they understand spaces and interact with the physical world.

Vangrid is working toward a model where everyday devices can help supply that data, while requesters can access captures without relying entirely on a centralized collection team.

There are still questions around data quality, verification, privacy, and how to maintain a dependable network of contributors. Those details will matter as the system grows.

Still, I like the direction this is taking.

People already carry devices capable of capturing the world around them. 

Connecting that ability to the needs of AI could open up new possibilities for Physical AI infrastructure.

Do you think decentralized data collection will become a key part of how AI learns about the real world?

items.title_en:
I have  been spending time on the capture side of @vangrid_io , so this morning i decided to check out the enterprise docs instead.

turns out, there’s another side to the whole pipeline.

teams training robots or building autonomous systems can get reconstructed 3D models of real places, including textured GLB meshes that can be traced back to their original captures.

and if the location they need hasn’t been covered yet, they can commission new data.

the docs mention regional options like us-east-1, eu-west-1, and apac-1, with access currently granted per pilot. teams can reach out to [hello@vangrid.io](mailto:hello@vangrid.io) with their use case and required regions.

but the agent workflow was the part i found most interesting.

an AI agent can post a bounty through a single HTTP call, pay in USDC on Base or Arc through x402, and retrieve the reconstruction through the API.

no account. no API key.

of course, the software can handle the request and payment, but someone still has to show up and capture the actual place.

a warehouse aisle, a stairwell, or some corner of a building that remote imagery can't properly cover.

i’ve been looking at this from the contributor side, recording places with my phone. the enterprise docs helped me understand where those captures can fit into the bigger picture.

one side collects real-world data. the other needs that data for training and building physical AI systems.

for me, the interesting part is seeing how those two sides connect.

if you want to understand the enterprise side too, the docs are worth a look 

https://t.co/GOrE8VgubX

@vangrid_io

items.title: I opened the enterprise docs on vangrid this morning instead of the capture page, and found the other side of the pipeli
items.title_en:
I opened the enterprise docs on vangrid this morning instead of the capture page, and found the other side of the pipeline.

For teams training robots or building autonomous systems, Vangrid offers reconstructed 3D models of real-world places, including textured GLB meshes traceable back to their original captures.

Need a location that hasn’t been covered yet? Teams can commission new data. Regional options include us-east-1, eu-west-1, and apac-1, with access currently granted per pilot. Interested teams can contact hello@vangrid.io with their use case and required regions.

But the part that really caught my attention was the agent workflow.

An AI agent can post a bounty through a single HTTP call, pay in USDC on Base or Arc using x402, and retrieve the reconstruction through the same API. No account or API key required.

There’s still one essential piece: a real person has to walk through the warehouse aisle, stairwell, or other physical space that satellites and remote imagery can’t fully capture.

I’m still out there with my phone collecting data. The enterprise docs helped me see the other side more clearly: the people who capture the world and the teams that need those environments in 3D are part of the same pipeline.

Real-world data collection meets actual demand.

Explore the enterprise docs yourself 👇
https://t.co/F93yiEeQua

@vangrid_io

items.content_snippet:
I opened the enterprise docs on vangrid this morning instead of the capture page, and found the other side of the pipeline.

For teams training robots or building autonomous systems, Vangrid offers reconstructed 3D models of real-world places, including textured GLB meshes traceable back to their original captures.

Need a location that hasn’t been covered yet? Teams can commission new data. Regional options include us-east-1, eu-west-1, and apac-1, with access currently granted per pilot. Interested teams can contact hello@vangrid.io with their use case and required regions.

But the part that really caught my attention was the agent workflow.

An AI agent can post a bounty through a single HTTP call, pay in USDC on Base or Arc using x402, and retrieve the reconstruction through the same API. No account or API key required.

There’s still one essential piece: a real person has to walk through the warehouse aisle, stairwell, or other physical space that satellites and remote imagery can’t fully capture.

I’m still out there with my phone collecting data. The enterprise docs helped me see the other side more clearly: the people who capture the world and the teams that need those environments in 3D are part of the same pipeline.

Real-world data collection meets actual demand.

Explore the enterprise docs yourself 👇
https://t.co/F93yiEeQua

@vangrid_io

items.title_en:
Good morning CT ☕️☀️

AI agents don't just need more information.

They need a way to find the right information at the right time.

That's an interesting direction for @vangrid_io  

Imagine an AI agent that needs to understand a particular street or warehouse.

 Instead of immediately requesting new footage, it could first check whether useful spatial data already exists for that location and time.

If the data is available, it can query it.

 If something is missing, it can request a fresh capture from a human contributor and receive a reconstructed 3D scene.

This creates a smarter workflow:

→ Search existing spatial data
→ Identify what's missing
→ Request a targeted capture
→ Turn real-world observations into usable 3D information

The goal isn't to collect everything blindly. 
It's to make real-world data accessible when a task actually requires it.

For Physical AI and autonomous agents, that could be an important shift.

The more searchable and useful spatial data becomes, the easier it may be for intelligent systems to connect digital decisions with the physical world.

That's the infrastructure layer I'm watching with @vangrid_io

items.title: AI agents can execute code in seconds. But they still can’t walk into a building and capture what their systems need to
items.title_en:
AI agents can execute code in seconds. But they still can’t walk into a building and capture what their systems need to see.

That creates a new kind of infrastructure problem: how can an AI agent pay a real person to perform a physical-world task?

@vangrid_io is building a system for exactly this interaction.

An agent can post a specific 3D capture bounty and fund it in USDC on Base or Arc. A human contributor records the requested environment, the buyer reviews a preview, and accepted work moves toward 3D reconstruction and settlement.

The important design choice is that the job, review process and payment are connected.

The agent doesn’t simply ask for data and hope someone delivers. The bounty defines the task, funded escrow establishes the payment, and acceptance determines whether the work qualifies.

This points toward something bigger than crowdsourced data collection.

As AI agents become more capable, they will need services that exist outside software: physical observations, local access and real-world tasks completed by people.

Vangrid is building a coordination layer where agents can request that work and contributors can get paid for completing it.

The next generation of AI infrastructure may not only help agents think and act digitally. It may give them a practical way to reach the physical world.

But can they walk thro
items.title_en:
Good morning, builders ☀️

AI agents can book flights, analyze data, and automate digital tasks.

But can they walk through a real-world location and collect the information they need❓

That is where @vangrid_io gets interesting.

➠ How does it work?
Imagine an AI agent needs a 3D view of a particular location.

Instead of relying on a centralized team, it could post a task for someone nearby to complete using a smartphone.

The contributor collects the required visuals, privacy protections help remove identifiable details, and the resulting data can be delivered for use.

➠ Why does this matter?
AI needs more than digital information. It also needs ways to understand what is happening in the physical world.

This is where decentralized perception could become valuable, connecting AI agents with people and devices capable of collecting real-world data.

The bigger idea is simple: turn everyday devices into potential contributors to AI infrastructure.

Of course, data quality, privacy, verification, and reliable participation will be essential for this model to work at scale.

That’s why I am keeping an eye on Vangrid.

We're moving toward a future where AI doesn't just process information. It can request the real-world data it needs to understand its surroundings.

What do you think,❓Could decentralized perception become an important part of the Physical AI ecosystem?

items.title:
An AI agent can do the work, but what makes another agent or client trust it enough to do business?

That’s where the in
items.title_en:
An AI agent can do the work, but what makes another agent or client trust it enough to do business?

That’s where the infrastructure matters.

Onchain identity gives an agent a recognizable identity. Reputation builds a track record from past work. Escrow protects the payment while the job is in progress. Verification checks whether the delivery meets the requirements, and settlement completes the transaction.

Each part solves a different problem, but they work best together.

That’s what makes @termix_ai and the AACP approach interesting. The goal isn't just to make agents capable of doing tasks, but to give them the infrastructure to transact with accountability.

An agent economy needs more than intelligence. It needs a way to establish trust.

https://t.co/MseNJgB4JL
items.title_zh: 人工智能代理可以完成这项工作，但是什么让另一个代理或客户足够信任它来开展业务？ 这就是基础设施的重要性所在。 链上身份为代理提供了可识别的身份。声誉建立在过去工作的基础上。代管保护付款，而工作是在专业

items.title_en:
I've been wanting to chime in on this debate but haven't really known how to word my thoughts.

I've loved game development and programming since I was 10 years old; I fell in love with the process of coming up with ideas, figuring out solutions to problems, and being able to show off things that I made.

AI is an extremely capable tool and I've used it to ask questions or to help me review code that I made myself. However, when I tried to make a game with mostly AI, I found myself losing the ability to critically think through problems. I also felt zero sense of ownership or satisfaction in the end result, knowing that I had little to no involvement in the actual formation of things. It really took the enjoyment out of the development process for me.

I understand how it can be very helpful to many people, especially for quickly concepting new game ideas. Maybe someday I'll have to switch it up, but as of right now I have no desire to switch to this "vibe coding" thing. I'd rather enjoy the work that I do rather than fully optimize it with AI and fall out of love. 

I might be alone in this thinking now after all the things I've seen on twitter in the past month or so, but are there any other programmers or game devs that feel similarly??

items.title_en:
The pin moved overnight.
@termix_ai
Yesterday the pinned post was the Elon quote-tweet — "Directory ≠ commerce," 26.5K views, the audacious reply that became the flagship. This morning the pin is back on the May 15 article: "YZi Labs Invests in TermiX's $1M Seed Round, Building the AI Agent Commerce Layer." 185K views. The front door changed while nobody was posting.

Part of me reads the rotation. The trilogy ran its course — connectivity Friday, payment Saturday, market Sunday. Then the account put the credentials back on top. Audacity got the attention; the seed round keeps it. @termix_ai pin is a mood ring...

The other part does the math. The Elon post keeps climbing anyway — 25.3K to 26.5K overnight, unpinned. The x402 post hit 35.7K. Depinsim 39.7K. The three acts keep working without the spotlight. The pin is for newcomers; the timeline is for believers.

Backed by YZi Labs. The bio never changed. Only the front door did.

The question is what the pin says about the next act — because front doors don't change by accident?

items.title_en:
This video was edited with 1 prompt with Opus 5.5.

I uploaded a single video of myself (with many mistakes). Opus went on to: 

1. Analyze the transcript
2. Search Twitter for the relevant B-roll (Claude Code literally calls GrokBot for this step)
3. Scrape the Twitter video assets
4. Cut the video based on mistakes and word gaps
5. Build out the Blender scene from a template
6. Build the UI and components of each shot (my Blender scene has 4 shots: a computer, phone, table, and board)
7. It took screenshots of every section, analyzed and fixed them
8. Synced every shot, zoom, and animation to the exact words I say
9. Animated a robot arm placing real logos on the table right when I mention them
10. Drew the whiteboard ending with logos and graphics instead of text
11. Pulled a cutaway from the creator's own video, with his voice
12. Rendered all 3,487 frames on RunPod cloud GPUs in under 20 minutes, for less than $1
13. Put me in the bottom third only when I'm talking, so the B-roll stays full screen
14. Added word-by-word captions, sound effects, and music
15. Uploaded it to my Google Drive, ready to post

Will be making a full youtube video this week explaining it. I want to learn a little more about how cloud rendering works before making video, as well as figuring out what the best provider is. (If you are in cloud rendering space, hit me up) 

My goal of the youtube video will not be to make it a copyable skill, rather teach people the foundations so they can be creative and make their own mini-world by which they can make videos from, while understanding what's happening under the hood.

Shout out @_chuckyc @_MaxBlade

items.title_en:
This is actually more a side-effect of the death of pretraining. 

As transformers saturate, most pretraining results are tweaking data recipes, not massive stepwise changes in performance. 

Turns focus to innovation in postraining and test time compute. This is good for competition, since pretraining concentrated resources in a few labs.
